entry.title: clustering from scratch, part 4: Gaussian mixtures and EM

link.title: clustering from scratch, part 4: Gaussian mixtures and EM

entry.content:
Series · Clustering from scratch 1k-means 2Hierarchical clustering 3DBSCAN and density 4Gaussian mixtures and EM

Every method so far has given each point a single, definite answer: this cluster, or noise. But some points really are ambiguous. A point exactly halfway between two blobs belongs to each about equally, and pretending otherwise throws information away.

Part 1 also left k-means with round clusters only. Real groups are often stretched, tilted, or of different sizes.

A Gaussian mixture model fixes both. It describes the data as a blend of a few Gaussian (bell-shaped) blobs, each with its own centre, its own shape and tilt, and its own share of the points. Fitting one gives every point a probability of belonging to each blob. The algorithm that fits it, EM, turns out to be a soft version of k-means.

The toy data

The figure starts with 78 points in three long, tilted blobs: two parallel ones at the top, very close together, and one flatter one below. The menu has the earlier datasets too. New start under the figure tries another starting guess.

Gaussian mixtures, step by step

First, k-means, the best of 10 starts with k = 3. It gets most points right, 92% agreement with the true groups, but look at the borders.

The two top blobs are long and tilted. k-means only knows distance to a centre, so its borders are straight lines halfway between centres, and they cut across the ends of the blobs. And every point gets one colour, even those that sit right on a border.

A 2-D Gaussian is a bell-shaped hill of probability. It’s described by two things:

  • its mean μ, the centre of the hill,
  • its covariance Σ, a 2 × 2 matrix that sets the hill’s width in each direction and its tilt.

The ellipses mark where the hill is 1 and 2 standard deviations from its centre (in 2-D, they contain about 39% and 86% of its points). Here a single Gaussian is fitted to all 78 points: mean (4.61, 5.10), and a covariance with 3.78 and 3.98 on its diagonal and 0.19 off it. Nearly round, because the three blobs together fill the square.

One Gaussian is a poor description of three blobs. A mixture of three should do better.

A mixture of k Gaussians says each point was made in two steps: first pick one of the k components at random, with probabilities \(\pi_1, \dots, \pi_k\) (the weights), then draw the point from that component’s Gaussian.

We don’t know any of the parameters, and we don’t know which component made which point. EM needs a starting guess. Here: three means picked by k-means++, each component given the covariance of the whole dataset, and equal weights of 1/3. That’s why the three ellipses start out the same size and nearly round.

E step. For each point, ask: given the current guesses, how likely is it that each component made this point? By Bayes’ rule, the answer for component j is proportional to its weight times its density at the point:

\[r_{ij} = \frac{\pi_j\, \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_j, \Sigma_j)}{\sum_m \pi_m\, \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_m, \Sigma_m)}\]

These are the responsibilities. Each point’s add up to 100%. The figure walks through the points: each one takes the colour of its most likely component, and the fainter it is, the less sure. The first point, (5.6, 9.0), is 73% component 2 and 26% component 1.

With such a rough start, almost everything is unsure: 77 of the 78 points are under 90% for any one component.

M step. Now refit each Gaussian, using every point, but counting each one by its responsibility. A point that is 73% component 2 counts as 0.73 of a point there and 0.26 of a point in component 1. So for component j:

  • its weight is its share of all the responsibility,
  • its mean is the responsibility-weighted average of the points,
  • its covariance is the responsibility-weighted spread around that mean.

It’s the k-means update step, with fractional members. The ellipses move, and start to stretch along their blobs.

Alternate the two steps. Better parameters give sharper responsibilities, which give better parameters.

The chart tracks the log-likelihood: how probable the whole dataset is under the current mixture, on a log scale. It rises after every round, from −342.16 at the start to −320.97 after the first M step, and never falls. Going deeper proves it can’t.

Watch the two top ellipses: they tilt to match their blobs, and narrow until they lie side by side.

EM stops when the log-likelihood stops improving. Here that’s after 17 rounds, at −246.27.

Each component found its blob’s shape: the two top ellipses are long and tilted, the bottom one long and flat. The assignment, taking each point’s most likely component, agrees with the true groups 100%, against 92% for k-means.

And the uncertainty is still there where it matters: the point at (3.1, 3.2), where the tail of a top blob reaches the bottom one, is only 88% sure. On stretched the mixture gets 100% where k-means got 78%.

More components always fit better, just as more centres always lowered the inertia in part 1. So the log-likelihood alone can’t pick k.

The Bayesian information criterion (BIC) adds a penalty for every parameter:

\[\text{BIC} = -2 \log L + p \log n\]

where p is the number of numbers the model needs. Lower is better. Each 2-D component costs 5 (2 for the mean, 3 for the covariance), plus one weight.

Move the slider, or keep scrolling. BIC is lowest at k = 3: 566.60, against 620.01 for 2 and 584.05 for 4.

Switch to two moons. A mixture of two Gaussians does no better than k-means here (57% against 64%): a moon isn’t an ellipse.

BIC is honest about it, though. On the moons it prefers 6 components to 2: the best description of a curved cluster, in Gaussians, is several overlapping ones. A mixture model describes where the points are dense; it doesn’t know which components “belong together”.

That’s the trade-off of the whole series. k-means and Gaussian mixtures assume a shape and are fast; hierarchical and density-based methods follow any shape, but need a distance threshold.

The whole thing in two lines

A mixture of \(k\) Gaussians gives a point \(x\) the density

\[p(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \pi_j\, \mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu_j, \Sigma_j), \qquad \mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, \Sigma) = \frac{\exp\!\big(-\tfrac{1}{2}(x - \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)\big)}{2\pi \sqrt{\det \Sigma}}\]

(that’s the 2-D version of the Gaussian), and EM fits it by repeating

\[\textbf{E:}\quad r_{ij} = \frac{\pi_j\, \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_j, \Sigma_j)}{\sum_m \pi_m\, \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_m, \Sigma_m)}\] \[\textbf{M:}\quad N_j = \sum_i r_{ij}, \quad \pi_j = \frac{N_j}{n}, \quad \mu_j = \frac{1}{N_j} \sum_i r_{ij}\, x_i, \quad \Sigma_j = \frac{1}{N_j} \sum_i r_{ij} (x_i - \mu_j)(x_i - \mu_j)^\top\]

until the log-likelihood \(\log L = \sum_i \log p(x_i)\) stops rising.

Side by side with k-means:

  k-means Gaussian mixture
a cluster is a centre a mean, a covariance and a weight
a point is in one cluster in every cluster, with a probability
borders are straight lines curves (conic sections)
step 1 assign to the nearest centre E: responsibilities by Bayes’ rule
step 2 centre = mean of members M: weighted mean, covariance and weight
it maximises −inertia log-likelihood

Wrapping up the series

Four algorithms, four answers to “what is a cluster?”:

  • k-means: points near the same centre. Fast and simple; round clusters of similar size.
  • Hierarchical: points joined by short links, at every scale at once. No k up front; slow on big data.
  • DBSCAN: points in the same crowded region. Any shape, and real noise; one density for everything.
  • Gaussian mixtures: points drawn from the same tilted bell curve. Soft answers and elliptical shapes; still blobs.

None is best everywhere, which is why scikit-learn’s comparison page shows a whole grid of them on toy datasets much like the ones here. The useful question is which assumption fits your data.

Going deeper

Why the log-likelihood never goes down

Write \(z_i\) for the (unknown) component that made point \(i\), and \(\theta\) for all the parameters. For any probabilities \(q_i(j)\) over the components, multiply and divide by \(q_i(j)\) inside the log-likelihood of one point:

\[\log p(x_i \mid \theta) = \log \sum_j q_i(j)\, \frac{p(x_i, z_i = j \mid \theta)}{q_i(j)} \ \ge\ \sum_j q_i(j) \log \frac{p(x_i, z_i = j \mid \theta)}{q_i(j)}\]

The inequality is Jensen’s: the log of an average is at least the average of the logs, because log is concave. Call the right side, summed over points, \(B(q, \theta)\). It’s a lower bound on \(\log L(\theta)\) for any \(q\).

The gap between the two sides is \(\sum_i \text{KL}\big(q_i \,\|\, p(z_i \mid x_i, \theta)\big)\), which is zero exactly when \(q_i\) is the posterior \(p(z_i = j \mid x_i, \theta)\), that is, the responsibilities. So:

  • E step: set \(q\) to the responsibilities under the current \(\theta_{old}\). Now \(B(q, \theta_{old}) = \log L(\theta_{old})\): the bound touches the curve.
  • M step: choose \(\theta_{new}\) to maximise \(B(q, \theta)\). Then
\[\log L(\theta_{new}) \ \ge\ B(q, \theta_{new}) \ \ge\ B(q, \theta_{old}) = \log L(\theta_{old})\]

The first \(\ge\) holds because \(B\) is a lower bound, the second because \(\theta_{new}\) maximises it. So the log-likelihood can’t go down. This is the general argument of Dempster, Laird and Rubin (1977), and it works for any model with hidden variables, not just Gaussian mixtures.

Where the M-step formulas come from

With \(q\) fixed, the part of \(B\) that depends on component \(j\) is

\[\sum_i r_{ij} \big(\log \pi_j + \log \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_j, \Sigma_j)\big)\]

The mean. \(\log \mathcal{N}\) contains \(-\tfrac{1}{2}(x_i - \mu_j)^\top \Sigma_j^{-1} (x_i - \mu_j)\), whose gradient in \(\mu_j\) is \(\Sigma_j^{-1}(x_i - \mu_j)\). Set the weighted sum to zero:

\[\Sigma_j^{-1} \sum_i r_{ij} (x_i - \mu_j) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \mu_j = \frac{\sum_i r_{ij}\, x_i}{\sum_i r_{ij}}\]

Part 1’s “why the mean”, with weights.

The weights. Maximise \(\sum_j N_j \log \pi_j\) subject to \(\sum_j \pi_j = 1\). With a Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda\), the derivative in \(\pi_j\) is \(N_j / \pi_j - \lambda = 0\), so \(\pi_j \propto N_j\), and the constraint gives \(\pi_j = N_j / n\).

The covariance. The same idea, differentiating with respect to \(\Sigma_j^{-1}\) (using \(\partial \log\det A / \partial A = A^{-\top}\)), gives the responsibility-weighted covariance.

k-means is EM in the limit

Fix every covariance to \(\sigma^2 I\) (round, all the same size) and every weight to \(1/k\). Then the responsibilities are

\[r_{ij} = \frac{\exp\!\big(-\lVert x_i - \mu_j \rVert^2 / 2\sigma^2\big)}{\sum_m \exp\!\big(-\lVert x_i - \mu_m \rVert^2 / 2\sigma^2\big)}\]

a softmax of minus the squared distances, at temperature \(2\sigma^2\). As \(\sigma \to 0\), the nearest centre’s term dominates every other, and \(r_{ij}\) becomes 1 for the nearest centre and 0 for the rest. The E step becomes k-means’ assign step, and the M step for the means becomes its update step. So k-means is “hard EM” for a mixture of tiny, identical, round Gaussians, which is why it likes round clusters of similar size.

The likelihood can be infinite

Put one component’s mean exactly on a data point, and shrink its covariance towards zero. Its density at that point grows without limit, so the log-likelihood goes to \(+\infty\). The “best” fit is a useless spike.

EM rarely walks into this from a sensible start, but it can, especially with many components and few points. The standard fix is to add a small number to the covariance’s diagonal at every M step. This page adds \(10^{-6}\), the same default as scikit-learn’s reg_covar. A more principled fix puts a prior on the covariances, which turns maximum likelihood into maximum a posteriori estimation.

Local maxima, again

EM only climbs. Like k-means, it stops at the top of whichever hill it started on. On the default points, 40 of 100 different starts end at a clearly lower log-likelihood than the best. Libraries run several starts (scikit-learn’s n_init) and keep the best, and usually start from a k-means solution.

Counting parameters for BIC

A 2-D component has 2 numbers in its mean and 3 in its covariance (it’s symmetric, so the two off-diagonal entries are the same number). The \(k\) weights add up to 1, so only \(k - 1\) are free. In total,

\[p = 5k + (k - 1) = 6k - 1\]

The \(\log n\) factor comes from Schwarz (1978): it’s what you get approximating the probability of the data under the model, averaged over all parameter values, for large \(n\). Its practical meaning: an extra parameter has to raise the log-likelihood by about \(\tfrac{1}{2} \log n\) to be worth it. With 78 points, that’s about 2.2 per parameter, or 13 per extra component.

Fewer parameters per component

A full covariance has \(d(d+1)/2\) numbers in \(d\) dimensions: 5,050 for \(d = 100\). With few points, that’s far too many to estimate. Common restrictions, as in scikit-learn’s covariance_type:

type each component’s shape numbers per covariance
full any ellipse, any tilt \(d(d+1)/2\)
diagonal an ellipse aligned with the axes \(d\)
spherical a circle (a sphere) 1
tied full, but the same for every component \(d(d+1)/2\), shared

Spherical, with equal weights and \(\sigma \to 0\), is k-means again.

Further reading

  • A. Dempster, N. Laird and D. Rubin, Maximum Likelihood from Incomplete Data via the EM Algorithm (1977): EM in general.
  • C. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (2006), chapter 9: mixtures, EM and the k-means connection, with the bound argument above.
  • G. Schwarz, Estimating the Dimension of a Model (1978): the BIC.
  • scikit-learn, Gaussian mixture models: covariance types, BIC model selection and a Bayesian variant that picks k by itself.

entry.title: clustering from scratch, part 3: DBSCAN and density

link.title: clustering from scratch, part 3: DBSCAN and density

entry.content:
Series · Clustering from scratch 1k-means 2Hierarchical clustering 3DBSCAN and density 4Gaussian mixtures and EM

Part 1 and part 2 both put every point in some cluster. Real data is rarely that tidy. Sensors glitch, people mistype, and some points simply don’t belong to any group. Forcing them into a cluster drags that cluster’s centre, or, as with single linkage, glues two clusters together through a thin bridge.

DBSCAN (Ester et al., 1996) takes a different view of what a cluster is: a region where points are crowded together, separated from other such regions by emptier space. Points in empty space aren’t forced anywhere. They are labelled noise.

The name stands for Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise. It needs two numbers from us instead of k:

  • ε (epsilon), a radius: how near counts as “nearby”,
  • minPts, a count: how many points within ε make a spot “crowded”.

It never asks how many clusters there are. That comes out of the data.

The toy data

The figure starts with three blobs of 20 points, plus 14 points scattered at random over the whole square. Those 14 belong to no group. The menu has the earlier datasets and two new ones: a blob inside a ring, and a dense blob next to a sparse one. The sliders under the figure set ε and minPts, and every step reruns on the spot.

DBSCAN, step by step

74 points: three blobs, and 14 points scattered at random over the square. Those 14 aren’t a cluster, and they aren’t part of any blob.

k-means would hand each of them to the nearest centre, pulling the centres off towards them. DBSCAN will leave most of them out.

Draw a circle of radius ε around a point and count the points inside it, the point itself included. With the defaults, ε = 1 and minPts = 5.

The figure tries three points as you scroll:

  • (2.7, 8.3), inside the top-left blob, has 5 points in its circle. That’s at least minPts, so it is a core point: it sits somewhere crowded.
  • (3.6, 5.9), at the edge of a blob, has only 3.
  • (3.9, 8.7), out in the open, has 2.

The last two are not core points. We’ll see in a moment that they end up very differently.

Do this for every point. The ringed points are the core points, each drawn with its ε-circle. Here 52 of the 74 points are core.

Together the circles map out the dense regions. Where circles overlap, those core points are in the same dense region. Most scattered points have no circle: there’s nothing near them.

Now build clusters. Take any core point that isn’t in a cluster yet, and start a new cluster with it. Then:

  • every point within ε of it joins the cluster,
  • each new point that is also core does the same, passing the cluster on to its own neighbours,
  • a new point that is not core joins, but passes nothing on.

When the cluster stops growing, start the next one from another unused core point. The lines show who brought whom into each cluster. It’s a flood fill: the cluster spreads as far as the crowd goes, and stops where the crowd thins out.

Some points joined without being core. They are within ε of a core point but don’t have minPts neighbours themselves. These are border points: the thin edge of a cluster. Here there are 8.

Border points matter because of the rule above: they can’t pass a cluster on. That’s what stops a cluster from leaking out along a sparse trail of points, the way single linkage did across the bridge in part 2.

Every point that is neither core nor within ε of a core is noise, drawn hollow. It belongs to no cluster.

With the defaults: 3 clusters, 52 core points, 8 border points and 14 noise points. 10 of the 14 scattered points are among the noise. The other 4 happened to land close enough to a blob to join it, which is fair: from the data alone, nothing marks them as different.

Nobody told DBSCAN there were three clusters. The count came from the density.

Now switch the dataset. A cluster is anything that’s connected through crowded space, so its shape doesn’t matter:

  • two moons: both moons found, 97% agreement with the true groups, against 64% for k-means. Two points are left as noise; ε = 1.2 gets all of them.
  • ring around a blob: the blob and the ring come out as two clusters, 100%. k-means can’t do this at all (50%): the ring’s centre is in the middle of the blob.

DBSCAN keeps single linkage’s ability to follow chains of neighbours, but it only follows chains through crowded points.

The price is choosing ε and minPts. Try the sliders. Small ε turns most points into noise. Large ε merges everything into one cluster.

A common guide is the k-distance plot on the right. For each point, find the distance to its minPts-th nearest point (counting itself), and sort these from largest to smallest. Points inside clusters have small values; noise points have large ones. Look for the knee where the curve flattens, and set ε near it.

The dashed line is the current ε. The 22 points above it can’t be core points.

Pick dense and sparse from the menu. One tight blob of 30 points, one loose blob of 30.

  • With ε = 0.5, the dense blob is found but 23 of the sparse blob’s 30 points are noise.
  • With ε = 1, the sparse blob comes out as two pieces, and one of them is glued onto the dense blob.
  • From ε = 1.3 up, the two blobs merge into a single cluster.

There’s no ε that gets both right, because DBSCAN uses one density threshold for the whole dataset. Here k-means does better (93%). Fixing this is what OPTICS and HDBSCAN are for. Going deeper has the idea.

The whole thing in a few definitions

For a point \(p\), write \(N_\varepsilon(p) = \{\, q : \lVert p - q \rVert \le \varepsilon \,\}\) for its ε-neighbourhood, which includes \(p\) itself.

  • \(p\) is a core point if \(\lvert N_\varepsilon(p) \rvert \ge \text{minPts}\).
  • \(q\) is directly reachable from \(p\) if \(p\) is core and \(q \in N_\varepsilon(p)\).
  • \(q\) is reachable from \(p\) if there’s a chain \(p = p_1, p_2, \dots, p_m = q\) where each step is directly reachable. All but the last point of the chain must be core.
  • A cluster is a core point together with everything reachable from it.
  • A noise point is one that isn’t reachable from any core point.

Reachability isn’t symmetric: a border point is reachable from a core point, but nothing is reachable from a border point. So the paper also defines two points as connected if both are reachable from some common core point, and a cluster is exactly a maximal set of connected points.

What’s still missing

  • ε and minPts. They are easier to reason about than k, but they still have to be chosen, and one pair has to fit the whole dataset.
  • Different densities. The last step showed DBSCAN can’t handle clusters that are crowded to different degrees.
  • High dimensions. In many dimensions, distances between random points all become similar, so a radius ε stops separating “near” from “far”.

None of the three methods so far says how sure it is about a point. A point halfway between two blobs gets a hard yes or no. Part 4, Gaussian mixtures, gives every point a probability of belonging to each cluster, and fits clusters that can be stretched and tilted.

Going deeper

Clusters are connected pieces of a graph

Join every pair of core points that are within ε of each other. That gives a graph on the core points. The clusters’ core points are exactly the connected components of this graph: two core points are in the same cluster when a chain of core points, each within ε of the next, links them. That’s the definition of reachability, restricted to core points.

Then each border point is attached to a component it is within ε of, and the points left over are noise. So DBSCAN is “find the connected components” plus a rule for the edges. That’s also why it doesn’t matter which core point a cluster grows from: the component is the same.

DBSCAN generalises single linkage

Set minPts = 2. Then a point is core as soon as it has one other point within ε. The core graph joins any two points within ε, and its components are the clusters you get by cutting the single-linkage tree at height ε. The only difference is that single linkage would call an isolated point a cluster of one, where DBSCAN calls it noise.

Raising minPts is what stops the chaining. A bridge one point wide has points with only two or three neighbours each, so they aren’t core, and the cluster can’t flow across. Try bridged blobs with ε = 1: at minPts = 2 the two blobs come out as one cluster of 32, and at minPts = 5 as two clusters of 16 and 15.

Border points depend on the order

The core points and the noise points don’t depend on the order DBSCAN visits points in. Border points can. A border point within ε of core points from two clusters joins whichever cluster reaches it first. That’s rare and only affects points on the edge, but it means DBSCAN isn’t perfectly deterministic. A variant called DBSCAN* sidesteps it by treating all border points as noise.

Choosing minPts

The original paper suggests minPts = 4 for 2-D data, and a common rule is minPts = 2 × the number of dimensions. Larger values make the method more robust to noise and give smoother clusters, at the cost of losing small clusters entirely. Schubert et al. (2017) revisit these choices and give practical advice for setting both parameters.

The k-distance plot works because of how the two kinds of points behave. Inside a cluster, the distance to the minPts-th neighbour is roughly the spacing between points, which is small and about the same for every point. For noise, it’s the distance across empty space, which is large. Sorted, the noise points form the steep start of the curve, and the cluster points the long flat tail. The knee is where one group ends.

How fast is it?

The work is in the neighbourhood queries: for each point, find everything within ε. Done naively, that’s \(n\) distances per query and \(O(n^2)\) overall, which is what this page does. With a spatial index (a grid, or a tree like a k-d tree), each query only looks at nearby points. When ε is small compared with the spread of the data, that’s much faster in practice. The original paper claimed \(O(n \log n)\) on average, but in the worst case, when ε is so large that every point neighbours every other, nothing beats \(O(n^2)\).

Handling different densities

DBSCAN draws one horizontal cut through the data’s density: above the threshold set by ε and minPts is cluster, below is noise. Two ideas fix the single cut.

OPTICS (Ankerst et al., 1999) records, for each point, the smallest ε at which it would become reachable. That gives an ordering of the points from which the DBSCAN result for every ε can be read off, much like cutting a dendrogram at any height.

HDBSCAN (Campello et al., 2013) goes further. Let \(\text{core}_k(p)\) be the distance from \(p\) to its k-th nearest neighbour, which is small in dense regions. HDBSCAN replaces every distance by the mutual reachability distance:

\[d_{mr}(a, b) = \max\big(\text{core}_k(a),\ \text{core}_k(b),\ \lVert a - b \rVert\big)\]

That pushes sparse points away from everything while leaving dense regions as they are. Then it runs single linkage on these distances, and instead of one horizontal cut, it picks the clusters that survive longest in the tree. Each cluster effectively gets its own ε.

Further reading

  • M. Ester, H.-P. Kriegel, J. Sander and X. Xu, A Density-Based Algorithm for Discovering Clusters in Large Spatial Databases with Noise (1996): the original DBSCAN paper.
  • E. Schubert, J. Sander, M. Ester, H.-P. Kriegel and X. Xu, DBSCAN Revisited, Revisited (2017): how to choose the parameters, and how fast it really is.
  • M. Ankerst, M. Breunig, H.-P. Kriegel and J. Sander, OPTICS: Ordering Points To Identify the Clustering Structure (1999).
  • L. McInnes, J. Healy and S. Astels, How HDBSCAN Works: an illustrated walk through HDBSCAN.

entry.title: clustering from scratch, part 2: hierarchical clustering

link.title: clustering from scratch, part 2: hierarchical clustering

entry.content:
Series · Clustering from scratch 1k-means 2Hierarchical clustering 3DBSCAN and density 4Gaussian mixtures and EM

Part 1 ended with three complaints about k-means: we had to choose k up front, the answer depended on a random start, and every cluster came out as a round blob.

Hierarchical clustering answers the first two. It has no random start: run it twice and you get the same answer. And it doesn’t produce one clustering. It produces all of them at once, from “every point alone” to “everything together”, nested inside each other as a tree. You choose k afterwards, by looking at the tree.

The idea fits in one sentence: start with every point as its own cluster, and keep merging the two closest clusters until only one is left. The interesting part is what “closest” means for two groups of points.

The toy data

This time the figure starts with 24 points, three blobs of 8, so you can follow every merge. The menu above the figure has bigger datasets too, including two new ones made for this part. New points draws a fresh sample, and clicking the plot adds a point.

Agglomerative clustering, step by step

Start with 24 clusters, one point each. That’s a perfectly valid clustering, just not a useful one.

On the right is the dendrogram, the tree we are about to grow. For now it’s only its 24 leaves along the bottom, one per point. Each merge will add a ⊓ shape joining two branches. The height of the ⊓ records how far apart the two clusters were when they merged.

Step 1: measure the distance between every pair of points, and find the smallest. With 24 points there are 24 × 23 / 2 = 276 pairs.

The closest pair is (6.8, 7.8) and (7.0, 7.8), only 0.17 apart. They merge into one cluster of two points. Now there are 23 clusters.

Then do it again: find the two closest clusters and merge them. The figure plays the first 8 merges. Each line on the plot joins the two closest points across a merge, and each new ⊓ in the dendrogram sits at the merge’s height.

Early merges are short: points that sit right next to each other. Notice that the heights only go up. Each merge uses up the closest pair that’s left, so the next one can’t be closer. Going deeper makes that precise.

But “the two closest clusters” hides a question. Once a cluster has several points, how far is it from another cluster?

This choice is called the linkage, and there are four common answers. Here are two groups from part-way through, blue and red:

  • single: the distance between the closest pair of points, one from each group (the solid line): 1.11.
  • complete: the distance between the farthest pair (the dashed line): 2.15.
  • average: the mean distance over all pairs across the groups: 1.59.
  • Ward: how much the inertia from part 1 would grow if the two merged: 1.63.

Use the linkage menu below the figure to switch. The figure shows the pair that linkage merges when four clusters are left, so each linkage picks a different pair.

Now play all 23 merges. Points keep the colour of the cluster they end up in once they stop being alone, so you can watch the blobs fill in.

Inside each blob, merges are short and quick. Merging two blobs takes a long jump. On the default points with single linkage, the last two merges happen at heights 2.97 and 3.05. Every merge before them is at most 1.11.

This is the finished dendrogram. It records the entire history: which clusters merged, in what order, and how far apart they were.

The long vertical stretches are the important part. A long stretch means a cluster survived a long time before merging with anything: it’s well separated from everything else. On the default points the biggest jump in height comes after merge 21, which leaves 3 clusters.

To get k clusters, cut the tree with a horizontal line. Every merge below the line stays. Every merge above it is undone. Each branch the line crosses is one cluster.

Move the slider, or keep scrolling, to try 1 to 8 clusters. Cutting where the branches are longest gives the most natural answer: here, 3.

Unlike k-means, changing k doesn’t rerun anything. The 4-cluster answer is the 3-cluster answer with one cluster split in two. That’s what hierarchical means.

On easy data, every linkage agrees. Switch the dataset with the menu above the figure, and the linkage with the menu below it, to see where they part ways:

  • two moons: single linkage gets both moons exactly right (100%), where k-means managed 64%. A chain of close neighbours can follow a curve.
  • bridged blobs: the same chains hurt it here. A thin line of points connects the blobs, so single linkage merges them early and leaves one stray point as the second “cluster”. This is called chaining.
  • stretched: single linkage follows each long line (100%); complete linkage cuts across them (67%).

Complete and average linkage prefer compact clusters, which makes them closer to k-means.

Ward linkage merges the pair of clusters whose union raises the inertia the least. That’s k-means’ own score, so Ward is a greedy, step-by-step attempt at the k-means problem.

The merge costs add up: on the default points, the first 21 Ward merges cost 17.08 in total, and the 3 clusters left have an inertia of exactly 17.08. k-means finds the same answer here. On harder data Ward ends up a little worse (40.54 against 36.77 on bridged blobs), because it can never undo a merge.

That’s why Ward’s result is often used as the starting point for k-means.

The whole thing in one loop

Agglomerative clustering with a linkage \(D(A, B)\) between clusters:

  1. Start with \(n\) clusters \(\{x_1\}, \dots, \{x_n\}\).
  2. Find the pair \(A \ne B\) with the smallest \(D(A, B)\).
  3. Replace \(A\) and \(B\) by \(A \cup B\), and record a merge at height \(D(A, B)\).
  4. Stop when one cluster is left. Otherwise go to 2.

The four linkages, for clusters \(A\) and \(B\) with means \(\mu_A\) and \(\mu_B\):

linkage \(D(A, B)\) tends to give
single \(\min_{a \in A,\, b \in B} \lVert a - b \rVert\) long chains; follows any shape
complete \(\max_{a \in A,\, b \in B} \lVert a - b \rVert\) compact clusters of similar diameter
average \(\frac{1}{\lvert A \rvert \lvert B \rvert} \sum_{a, b} \lVert a - b \rVert\) between the two
Ward \(\frac{\lvert A \rvert \lvert B \rvert}{\lvert A \rvert + \lvert B \rvert} \lVert \mu_A - \mu_B \rVert^2\) round clusters, like k-means

What’s still missing

Hierarchical clustering solved two of part 1’s complaints, but not the rest.

  • It’s slow. The plain algorithm keeps all \(n^2 / 2\) pairwise distances in memory. That’s fine for thousands of points and hopeless for millions.
  • Merges are final. One bad early merge can never be undone.
  • Noise. Every point ends up in some cluster, even a lone point far from everything. On bridged blobs that’s what broke single linkage.

Single linkage’s success on the moons is a hint, though. It worked because it grows clusters through chains of close neighbours. Part 3, DBSCAN, keeps that idea, adds a rule that a cluster must be dense, and gets a proper notion of noise.

Going deeper

Why the heights only go up

Say \(A\) and \(B\) were the closest pair of clusters, so they merged at height \(h = D(A, B)\), and every other pair is at least \(h\) apart. Is the new cluster \(A \cup B\) also at least \(h\) from every other cluster \(C\)?

  • single: \(D(A \cup B, C) = \min\big(D(A, C), D(B, C)\big)\). Both are at least \(h\), so the minimum is too.
  • complete: \(D(A \cup B, C) = \max\big(D(A, C), D(B, C)\big) \ge h\), for the same reason.
  • average: \(D(A \cup B, C) = \frac{\lvert A \rvert\, D(A, C) + \lvert B \rvert\, D(B, C)}{\lvert A \rvert + \lvert B \rvert}\), a weighted average of two numbers at least \(h\).

So the next merge can’t happen below \(h\), and the heights never decrease. Ward linkage has the same property, by a longer calculation.

Not every linkage is this well behaved. Centroid linkage measures the distance between the clusters’ means. Take three points at the corners of an equilateral triangle with side 1. Two of them merge at height 1. Their mean is the midpoint of that side, which is only \(\sqrt{3}/2 \approx 0.87\) from the third point. So the next merge is lower than the one before it. That’s called an inversion, and it makes the dendrogram impossible to cut cleanly.

One update rule for every linkage

Recomputing \(D(A \cup B, C)\) from all the points would be slow. Lance and Williams (1967) noticed that every common linkage can be updated from the old cluster distances alone:

\[D(A \cup B, C) = \alpha_A D(A, C) + \alpha_B D(B, C) + \beta\, D(A, B) + \gamma\, \lvert D(A, C) - D(B, C) \rvert\]

with different coefficients for each linkage. For single linkage, \(\alpha_A = \alpha_B = \tfrac{1}{2}\), \(\beta = 0\) and \(\gamma = -\tfrac{1}{2}\). Check it: \(\tfrac{1}{2}(x + y) - \tfrac{1}{2}\lvert x - y \rvert = \min(x, y)\). Complete linkage is the same with \(\gamma = +\tfrac{1}{2}\), which gives \(\max(x, y)\). The figure above uses this rule: one update per remaining cluster per merge.

Ward’s cost is the growth in inertia

Part 1 showed that for a cluster with mean \(\bar{x}\), moving the centre to any other point \(\mu\) adds exactly \(m \lVert \bar{x} - \mu \rVert^2\) to its inertia, where \(m\) is its size. Now merge \(A\) and \(B\). The new mean is

\[\mu = \frac{\lvert A \rvert\, \mu_A + \lvert B \rvert\, \mu_B}{\lvert A \rvert + \lvert B \rvert}\]

Measured from the new mean, \(A\)’s points cost \(\lvert A \rvert \lVert \mu_A - \mu \rVert^2\) more than before, and \(B\)’s cost \(\lvert B \rvert \lVert \mu_B - \mu \rVert^2\) more. Write \(a = \lvert A \rvert\), \(b = \lvert B \rvert\) and \(\delta = \mu_A - \mu_B\). Then \(\mu_A - \mu = \frac{b}{a + b}\,\delta\) and \(\mu_B - \mu = -\frac{a}{a + b}\,\delta\), so the total increase is

\[a \frac{b^2}{(a + b)^2} \lVert \delta \rVert^2 + b \frac{a^2}{(a + b)^2} \lVert \delta \rVert^2 = \frac{ab\,(a + b)}{(a + b)^2} \lVert \delta \rVert^2 = \frac{ab}{a + b} \lVert \mu_A - \mu_B \rVert^2\]

That’s the Ward distance. Every point starts with inertia 0, and each merge adds its cost, so the inertia of the clusters left after any number of merges is the sum of the costs so far. That’s the 17.08 = 17.08 in the last step.

Ward is still greedy. Each merge is the cheapest one available now, which is not always the cheapest path to k clusters. That’s why it can end above the best k-means answer.

Single linkage is a minimum spanning tree

A spanning tree connects all the points with \(n - 1\) edges and no loops. The minimum spanning tree (MST) is the one with the smallest total edge length. Kruskal’s algorithm builds it greedily: go through all pairs in order of distance, and keep an edge whenever it joins two pieces that aren’t connected yet.

That’s single linkage exactly. Two clusters’ single-linkage distance is their closest pair, so “merge the two closest clusters” is “add the shortest edge that joins two pieces”. The lines drawn on the plot during the merges are the edges of the MST (Gower and Ross, 1969).

So cutting the single-linkage tree into k clusters is the same as deleting the k − 1 longest edges of the MST. This is also why it chains: one short edge is all it takes to join two groups, however thin the bridge.

The tree is a distance

The dendrogram defines a new distance between points: the cophenetic distance \(c(x, y)\), the height at which \(x\) and \(y\) first end up in the same cluster. It satisfies a stronger rule than the triangle inequality:

\[c(x, z) \le \max\big(c(x, y),\, c(y, z)\big)\]

To see why, let \(h = \max(c(x, y), c(y, z))\). At height \(h\), \(x\) is in the same cluster as \(y\), and \(y\) in the same cluster as \(z\). So all three are in one cluster, and \(x\) met \(z\) at height \(h\) or below. A distance with this property is called an ultrametric. Hierarchical clustering can be seen as replacing the real distances with the closest ultrametric, for some meaning of “closest” that depends on the linkage.

How slow is it?

The plain loop above does, for each of its \(n - 1\) merges, a search over up to \(n^2/2\) pairs: \(O(n^3)\) time, and \(O(n^2)\) memory for the distances. Smarter versions do better. Single linkage can be done in \(O(n^2)\) time and \(O(n)\) memory (Sibson, 1973), and Müllner (2011) describes fast algorithms for the others. But anything that looks at every pair is at least \(O(n^2)\), which is about 5 × 10¹¹ distances for a million points.

Top-down instead of bottom-up

Everything here was agglomerative: bottom-up, merging. The other direction, divisive clustering, starts with one cluster and keeps splitting it. One simple version is bisecting k-means: run k-means with k = 2 on the biggest cluster, and repeat. It’s fast, since each split is a cheap k-means run, and it gives a tree too, but its splits are only as good as k-means is on each piece.

Further reading

  • J. Ward, Hierarchical Grouping to Optimize an Objective Function (1963): the Ward criterion.
  • G. Lance and W. Williams, A General Theory of Classificatory Sorting Strategies (1967): the one update rule for all linkages.
  • R. Sibson, SLINK: an optimally efficient algorithm for the single-link cluster method (1973).
  • D. Müllner, Modern hierarchical, agglomerative clustering algorithms (2011): fast algorithms for every linkage, and the basis of SciPy’s implementation.
  • SciPy, scipy.cluster.hierarchy.linkage: every linkage here, plus dendrogram plotting.

entry.title: clustering from scratch, part 1: k-means
entry.content:
Series · Clustering from scratch 1k-means 2Hierarchical clustering 3DBSCAN and density 4Gaussian mixtures and EM

Give someone a scatter of dots and ask them to circle the groups. Most people can do it in a second. Clustering is the problem of getting a computer to do the same: split a set of points into groups, when nobody has told it what the groups are or even how many there are.

That last part is what makes it hard. In classification, every training point comes with the right answer. In clustering there is no answer key. An algorithm has to decide for itself what “a group” means, and each algorithm in this series decides differently.

This series builds four classic algorithms, one per part. Every figure runs the real algorithm in your browser on the points it shows, and every number you see is computed, not drawn by hand. This first part covers the oldest and most widely used: k-means.

The toy data

The main figure starts with 60 points in a 10 × 10 square, drawn from three round blobs of 20 points each. The algorithm is never told which blob a point came from. We only use that at the very end, to check its answer.

Above the figure you can:

  • switch to another dataset (big and small, stretched, two moons),
  • press new points to draw a fresh sample,
  • click anywhere in the plot to add a point of your own.

Every step below reruns on whatever data is on screen. Scroll slowly: inside each step, scrolling also plays the step.

k-means, step by step

Here is the input: 60 points, each just a pair of numbers (x, y). There are no labels and no colours.

Your eye probably finds three groups straight away. k-means needs one thing from us before it can start: k, the number of clusters to look for. Here k = 3. We will come back to the question of how to pick k at the end.

Each cluster will be summarised by one point, its centre. Finding good centres is the whole job.

We have to start somewhere. The simplest choice, used since the 1960s, is to pick k of the data points at random and call them the centres. (It’s often called the Forgy start.)

This start is not a good one. Two of the three centres landed in the same blob at the top right, and the bottom blob got none. Keep an eye on whether the algorithm recovers.

The button below the figure, new start, picks another random start.

Step 1 of every round: assign. For each point, measure the straight-line distance to every centre, and give the point the colour of the nearest one.

The figure walks through the points one at a time. The dashed lines are the distances; the solid one is the winner. The first point, at (2.7, 8.5), is 4.11 from c1, 1.89 from c2 and 4.87 from c3, so it joins c2.

Once every point is done, the tinted regions show each centre’s territory: every spot in a region is closer to that centre than to any other. The borders between them are straight lines. Going deeper says why.

Step 2: update. Each centre now moves to the mean of the points that chose it: the average of their x values and the average of their y values.

The lines show how far each centre travels. The bottom blob has no centre of its own, so its points split between c1 and c2, far above them, and both get dragged down towards it.

Why the mean, and not, say, the median? Because the mean is exactly the spot that makes the squared distances to the cluster’s points as small as possible. The proof is three lines.

Then we do it again. New centres mean some points now have a different nearest centre, so we reassign, then move the centres again, and so on.

The chart on the right tracks the inertia: the sum, over all points, of the squared distance from each point to its own centre. It is the score k-means is trying to make small.

Watch the chart as you scroll. The inertia goes down at every single step, both after an assign (a1, a2, …) and after an update (u1, u2, …). It never goes up. That’s not luck; it can’t.

When an assign step changes no colours, we’re done. The centres would move to the same means as last time, so nothing will ever change again.

On these points it takes 5 rounds. The inertia fell from 665.51 after the first assignment to 84.54.

And the algorithm did recover from its bad start: c1, which began in the top-right blob next to c3, worked its way down to the empty bottom blob over three rounds.

Here is a different random start on the same points. It also converges, but to a worse answer: one blob split in two, and two blobs sharing one centre.

Each step still lowered the inertia. The trouble is that the algorithm only ever looks for a small improvement nearby. Once no single reassignment helps, it stops, even if a much better answer exists elsewhere. That’s a local minimum.

On the default points, 13 of 100 random starts get stuck like this. The usual fix is to run k-means several times from different starts and keep the run with the lowest inertia.

A smarter start fixes most of this. k-means++ (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, 2007) picks the first centre at random, then picks each next one with probability proportional to D(x)²: the squared distance from a point to its nearest centre so far.

In the figure, each point’s size shows its chance of being picked. Points close to an existing centre shrink to almost nothing. Points far from every centre are the likely picks, so the starts tend to land in different blobs.

On the default points, k-means++ gets stuck in 1 of 100 starts, against 13 for plain random starts. It’s the default in scikit-learn and most other libraries.

We told k-means k = 3. What if we hadn’t known? Move the slider (or keep scrolling) to try every k from 1 to 8.

The top chart is the inertia of the best run for each k. It always falls as k grows, because more centres can always sit closer to the points. With k = 60, every point would be its own centre and the inertia would be 0. So “lowest inertia” can’t choose k.

Look for the elbow instead: the k after which adding a centre stops helping much. Here inertia drops from 595 to 296 to 85, then only to 71.

The lower chart is the silhouette, which asks whether each point sits closer to its own cluster than to the next nearest one. It peaks at 0.67, at k = 3. Going deeper has the formula.

Now switch the dataset with the menu above the figure.

On three blobs, k-means agrees with the true groups on 100% of pairs of points. Try the others:

  • big and small: k-means splits the big blob and lumps the small ones together, because it prefers clusters of similar size (90% of pairs).
  • stretched: three long, thin groups get cut across, because k-means wants round clusters (78%).
  • two moons: two curved groups get sliced down the middle by a straight line (64%).

Each failure comes from the same place: k-means describes a cluster by a single centre, so every cluster is a convex, roundish blob. The next three parts each drop part of that assumption.

The whole thing in one line

k-means looks for k centres \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_k\) and an assignment \(c_i\) of every point \(x_i\) to one of them that make the inertia small:

\[J = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lVert x_i - \mu_{c_i} \rVert^2\]

Lloyd’s algorithm makes it small by fixing one half of the unknowns and solving for the other half, over and over:

  1. Assign. Keep the centres fixed, and give each point its nearest one: \(c_i = \arg\min_j \lVert x_i - \mu_j \rVert^2\).
  2. Update. Keep the assignment fixed, and move each centre to the mean of its points: \(\mu_j = \frac{1}{\lvert C_j \rvert} \sum_{i \in C_j} x_i\).
  3. Stop when step 1 changes nothing.

Stuart Lloyd described it at Bell Labs in 1957 as a way to compress signals, though it was only published in 1982. James MacQueen gave it the name k-means in 1967.

Each round costs very little. With \(n\) points in \(d\) dimensions:

step work in our toy
assign \(n \cdot k\) distances, \(d\) terms each 60 × 3 = 180 distances
update one pass over the points 60 additions
one round about \(n\,k\,d\) about 360

That’s why k-means is still the first thing people try on millions of points.

What’s still missing

Three things should bother you.

  • We had to choose k. The elbow and the silhouette help, but they are rules of thumb run after the fact.
  • The answer depends on the start. Restarts and k-means++ make bad answers rare, not impossible.
  • Every cluster is a round blob. Clusters of very different sizes, stretched clusters and curved clusters all come out wrong.

Part 2, hierarchical clustering, doesn’t need k up front: it builds every possible number of clusters at once, as a tree. It has no random start, either.

Going deeper

The steps above show what k-means does. This section is about why. Each question stands on its own, so skip to the ones you care about.

Why the mean?

Take one cluster with points \(x_1, \dots, x_m\), and look for the single point \(\mu\) that makes the sum of squared distances smallest:

\[f(\mu) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \lVert x_i - \mu \rVert^2\]

\(f\) is a bowl (a sum of squares), so its lowest point is where its gradient is zero. The gradient of \(\lVert x_i - \mu \rVert^2\) with respect to \(\mu\) is \(-2(x_i - \mu)\), so

\[\nabla f(\mu) = -2 \sum_{i=1}^{m} (x_i - \mu) = -2\Big(\sum_{i=1}^m x_i - m\,\mu\Big) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \mu = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} x_i\]

the mean. There is a neater way to see it, which also says how much worse any other point is. Add and subtract the mean \(\bar{x}\) inside each term:

\[\sum_i \lVert x_i - \mu \rVert^2 = \sum_i \lVert (x_i - \bar{x}) + (\bar{x} - \mu) \rVert^2 = \sum_i \lVert x_i - \bar{x} \rVert^2 + m\,\lVert \bar{x} - \mu \rVert^2\]

The cross term \(2(\bar{x} - \mu) \cdot \sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})\) vanishes, because the points’ offsets from their mean add up to zero. So putting the centre anywhere other than the mean costs exactly \(m\) times the squared distance from the mean.

Try it on six numbers on a line. Drag the slider to move the centre: the cost is a parabola, and its lowest point is the mean.

Squared distance is what makes the answer the mean. If you used plain distance, \(\sum_i \lVert x_i - \mu \rVert\), the best single point would be the median instead (on a line), and the algorithm would be k-medians. It is less thrown by outliers, but the update step is harder to compute in more than one dimension.

Why the borders are straight lines

When is a point \(x\) exactly as far from centre \(a\) as from centre \(b\)? Write out both squared distances:

\[\lVert x - a \rVert^2 = \lVert x - b \rVert^2\] \[\lVert x \rVert^2 - 2\,a \cdot x + \lVert a \rVert^2 = \lVert x \rVert^2 - 2\,b \cdot x + \lVert b \rVert^2\]

The \(\lVert x \rVert^2\) cancels, and what’s left is

\[2\,(b - a) \cdot x = \lVert b \rVert^2 - \lVert a \rVert^2\]

That’s a straight line (in more dimensions, a flat plane), at right angles to the segment from \(a\) to \(b\) and through its midpoint. Each centre’s territory is what’s left after cutting the plane with one such line for each other centre. These regions are called Voronoi cells, and a region cut out by straight lines is always convex: the segment between any two points inside it stays inside.

That is the root of the failures in the last step. A curved moon isn’t convex, so no k-means cluster can be shaped like one.

Why it always stops

Each half of a round can only lower the inertia \(J\), or leave it alone:

  • Assign. Each point moves to its nearest centre, so its own term \(\lVert x_i - \mu_{c_i} \rVert^2\) can only shrink.
  • Update. Each centre moves to its cluster’s mean, which by the result above is the best spot for that cluster.

So \(J\) never goes up. And there are only finitely many ways to split \(n\) points into \(k\) groups (fewer than \(k^n\)). Every round either lowers \(J\), and so reaches an assignment it can never return to, or changes nothing and stops. So the algorithm must stop after finitely many rounds.

“Finitely many” can still be a lot. Vattani (2011) built point sets in the plane on which Lloyd’s algorithm needs exponentially many rounds. In practice it almost always stops in a few dozen, as on our points.

The stopping point is a local minimum: no single step improves it. Finding the best answer of all, the global minimum, is much harder. It is NP-hard even for k = 2 (Aloise et al., 2009), and even in the plane (Mahajan et al., 2012). So every practical method settles for good local minima.

How often do starts get stuck?

Below, k-means runs 200 times on the default points from plain random starts, and 200 times from k-means++ starts. Each bar counts how many runs ended at that inertia.

Arthur and Vassilvitskii proved that k-means++ is good in expectation, before Lloyd’s algorithm even runs. Write \(J_{opt}\) for the best inertia possible. Then the inertia of the k-means++ start alone satisfies

\[\mathbb{E}[J] \le 8\,(\ln k + 2)\, J_{opt}\]

For k = 3 that bound is about 25 times the best: loose, but it holds for every dataset, while a plain random start can be arbitrarily bad. The intuition is the D² weighting. A blob with no centre yet is far from every centre, so its points carry most of the probability. Lloyd’s rounds then only improve on the start.

Inertia as a sum over pairs

There’s a second way to write a cluster’s inertia, without any centre at all. For a cluster \(C\) with mean \(\bar{x}\):

\[\sum_{i \in C} \lVert x_i - \bar{x} \rVert^2 = \frac{1}{2\,\lvert C \rvert} \sum_{i \in C} \sum_{j \in C} \lVert x_i - x_j \rVert^2\]

To check it, expand \(\lVert x_i - x_j \rVert^2 = \lVert (x_i - \bar{x}) - (x_j - \bar{x}) \rVert^2\) and sum over both \(i\) and \(j\). The cross terms vanish for the same reason as before, and each of the two square terms gives \(\lvert C \rvert\) times the inertia.

So k-means is really asking for groups whose members are close to each other, on average, measured with squared distance. Part 2 will build clusters directly from distances between pairs of points.

More clusters always lower the inertia

Take the best clustering with \(k\) centres, and add a \((k+1)\)-th centre on top of any data point. Run one assign step. No point gets further from its centre, since it can only switch to the new one if that is closer, and the point under the new centre now costs 0. So the best inertia with \(k + 1\) centres is never higher than with \(k\), and strictly lower unless every point already sits on its centre.

That’s why inertia alone can’t pick k. Every rule for choosing k has to trade inertia against the number of clusters somehow.

The silhouette

For one point \(i\), let

  • \(a(i)\) be its mean distance to the other points in its own cluster,
  • \(b(i)\) be its mean distance to the points of the nearest other cluster.

Its silhouette (Rousseeuw, 1987) is

\[s(i) = \frac{b(i) - a(i)}{\max\big(a(i),\, b(i)\big)}\]

which lies between −1 and 1. Near 1, the point is much closer to its own cluster than to any other. Near 0, it sits on a border. Negative, it’s probably in the wrong cluster. The score of a whole clustering is the mean of \(s(i)\) over all points.

Unlike inertia, the silhouette doesn’t simply improve with k: split a real blob in two, and its points find the other half as close as their own, so \(b(i)\) drops towards \(a(i)\). That’s why it peaked at the true k = 3 here. It’s still a heuristic: it favours round, well-separated clusters, which is exactly what k-means produces anyway.

Scale changes the answer

k-means only sees distances, so the units of each coordinate matter. Measure height in millimetres and weight in kilograms, and height differences will dominate every distance; switch to metres and weight will. The clusters change with the units.

The usual fix is to standardise each feature first (subtract its mean, divide by its standard deviation), so each one counts about equally. That’s a choice, not a law: if one feature really matters more, leaving it bigger is a way of saying so.

k-means is a special case of a mixture model

Suppose each cluster is a round Gaussian blob, all with the same small spread \(\sigma\), and each point is drawn from one blob. Then the log-likelihood of a point under blob \(j\) is, up to a constant,

\[\log p(x \mid j) = -\frac{\lVert x - \mu_j \rVert^2}{2\sigma^2}\]

Picking the most likely blob for each point is picking the nearest centre, and fitting each blob’s mean to its points is the update step. Part 4 drops the “same, round, and hard choice” parts of that story, and gets Gaussian mixtures and the EM algorithm, which reduces to k-means as \(\sigma \to 0\).

Making it faster

On big datasets the assign step is the cost: \(n \cdot k\) distances per round. Two common speed-ups:

  • Skip distances you don’t need. If a point is very close to its centre, and that centre is far from every other centre, the point can’t switch. Elkan (Using the triangle inequality to accelerate k-means, 2003) uses the triangle inequality to skip most distance computations without changing the answer.
  • Use a sample. Mini-batch k-means (Sculley, 2010) updates the centres from a small random batch of points each round. It gives slightly worse answers, much faster.

Further reading

  • S. Lloyd, Least squares quantization in PCM (1982, written in 1957): the original algorithm.
  • D. Arthur and S. Vassilvitskii, k-means++: The Advantages of Careful Seeding (2007): the D² start and its guarantee.
  • P. Rousseeuw, Silhouettes: a graphical aid to the interpretation and validation of cluster analysis (1987).
  • scikit-learn, Clustering: a side-by-side comparison of many clustering algorithms on toy datasets like these.
  • Chris Piech, K Means: short Stanford CS221 notes covering the same ground.

link.title: attention is all you need, part 5: inference and the KV cache

entry.content:
Series · Attention is all you need 1Self-attention from scratch 2Multi-head attention and positions 3One encoder block 4The decoder, masking and training 5Inference and the KV cache

Part 4 finished the model: the decoder writes one word at a time, feeding each word back in. That loop is correct, but done naively it is slow. Every new word reruns the decoder over everything written so far.

This part is about inference: using a trained model, rather than training it. Almost everything that makes today’s chat models fast to run comes from one observation: with a causal mask, old positions never change. So their keys and values can be stored once and reused. That store is the KV cache.

Then we’ll look at the two main ways models shrink that cache, by sharing keys and values between heads (multi-query and grouped-query attention) and by limiting which past words a query may read (sliding windows and other attention patterns).

The scrolly figure below runs the decoder from part 4, with the cache, on the sentence you type. Every number is real.

The KV cache, step by step

Part 4’s generation loop, counted. At step \(k\), the decoder reads \(k\) tokens and computes queries, keys and values for all \(k\) of them, in every layer. Only the last position’s output is used to pick the next word.

Each row of the grid is one step; each cell is one position the decoder has to compute. Writing \(n\) words costs

\[1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}\]

positions: the work grows with the square of the length.

The mask makes old positions frozen. Position \(i\) only reads positions \(0 \dots i\). When a new word arrives at the end, nothing before it changes: the keys and values of the earlier positions come out exactly as they did last step.

So keep them. At each step, compute the keys and values of the new token only, append them to a cache, and let its query read the whole cache. The grid shrinks to its diagonal: \(n\) positions instead of \(n(n+1)/2\).

Cross-attention’s keys and values never change. They come from the encoder’s output, and the encoder reads the source sentence once. So before writing a single word, the decoder computes \(K = \text{memory} \cdot W_K\) and \(V = \text{memory} \cdot W_V\) for each layer and head, and keeps them for the whole generation.

Running the whole prompt through the model in one pass before writing is called prefill. In a decoder-only model like GPT, the prompt goes through the decoder itself, and prefill fills its self-attention cache with one row per prompt token.

A decode step. The decoder is fed a single token: the word it picked last step, plus the positional encoding for its place in the sentence. (Not position 0. A real implementation has to keep count.)

That one row of 8 numbers goes through \(W_Q\), \(W_K\) and \(W_V\) as in part 1, giving one query, one key and one value: each a single row of 4 numbers.

Append, don’t recompute. The new key goes to the bottom of the key cache, the new value to the bottom of the value cache. The rows above are what earlier steps put there, untouched.

This happens in every self-attention head of every decoder layer. The figure shows layer 1, head 1. Scroll on to watch it fill.

Attention with a single query. The new query is scored against every cached key, its own included:

\[\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{q K_{\text{cache}}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V_{\text{cache}}\]

That’s equation (1) from part 1 with a \(1 \times 4\) query instead of an \(n \times 4\) one. No mask is needed: the cache only holds the past.

The rest of the block (Add & Norm, cross-attention, the feed-forward network) also runs on just this one row.

The cache is not an approximation. The table runs both versions on your sentence: part 4’s full pass at every step, and the cached decode step. They pick the same words with the same probabilities, down to the last digit.

The trade: we’ve swapped repeated computation for memory. That memory is what the rest of this post is about.

The full cache. Every self-attention head in every decoder layer keeps a K and a V. In our toy that’s 2 layers × 2 heads × (4 + 4) numbers = 32 numbers per token.

In a real model it’s far more. Llama 2 7B keeps 2 × 32 layers × 32 heads × 128 = 262,144 numbers per token: half a megabyte at 16 bits. A 4,096-token conversation needs 2 GiB of cache on top of the weights.

Sharing keys and values between heads

The paper gives every attention head its own \(W_K\) and \(W_V\), so every head caches its own keys and values. That’s multi-head attention (MHA). But heads are mostly free to differ in their queries: what each one looks for. Do they each need their own keys and values?

  • Multi-query attention (MQA, Shazeer, 2019): all query heads share a single key head and a single value head. The cache shrinks by the number of heads, often 32× or more. Quality can drop somewhat.
  • Grouped-query attention (GQA, Ainslie et al., 2023): the middle ground. Query heads are split into groups, and each group shares one key and value head. With 8 groups, the authors found quality close to multi-head attention with speed close to multi-query.

Each query head still computes its own scores and weights; only the \(K\) and \(V\) they read are shared. Most open models since 2023 use GQA: Llama 2 70B, Llama 3, Mistral 7B and others pair 32 or 64 query heads with 8 key/value heads.

How much memory is that? For one sequence, the cache holds

\[2 \cdot L \cdot h_{kv} \cdot d_{head} \cdot n \cdot b \text{ bytes}\]

where the 2 is for K and V, \(L\) is the number of layers, \(h_{kv}\) the number of key/value heads, \(d_{head}\) the numbers per head, \(n\) the tokens so far and \(b\) the bytes per number (2, for 16-bit numbers).

Pick a model, a context length and a number of sequences served at once:

Try Llama 2 7B at its full 4,096 tokens and 32 sequences: 64 GiB of cache, for a model whose weights take about 13.5 GB. At long contexts the cache, not the model, decides how much a GPU can serve.

Which keys a query may read

So far we’ve met two attention patterns. The encoder’s self-attention is full: every word reads every word. The decoder’s is causal: every word reads only itself and the past. Cross-attention is a third kind: queries from one sequence, keys and values from another.

Patterns are just masks: which (query, key) pairs get a score, and which get \(-\infty\) (part 4). Changing the mask changes both the cost and what the cache has to keep. Rows are queries, columns are keys, and dark cells are pairs that get computed:

  • Sliding window (Longformer, Mistral 7B): each token reads only the last \(w\) tokens. Cost per token is fixed, and the cache can be a ring buffer of \(w\) rows. Information from further back still flows, but indirectly: layer 2 reads tokens that read the \(w\) before them, so after \(L\) layers a token can be influenced by about \(L \times w\) positions.
  • Attention sinks (StreamingLLM): trained models put a lot of attention on the first few tokens, whatever they are, as a place to park weight they don’t need. Evict those from a sliding window and the model falls apart. Keep the first 4 plus the window, and the authors ran Llama 2 stably on 4 million tokens.
  • Prefix (studied in the T5 paper): the prompt attends in both directions, like an encoder, and only the answer is causal. It’s a halfway house between the paper’s encoder–decoder and a decoder-only model.
  • Sparse patterns (Child et al., 2019): each token reads a local window plus every \(k\)-th earlier token, so two hops can reach anywhere at a cost of about \(n\sqrt{n}\) instead of \(n^2\).

Some models mix them. Gemma 2 alternates sliding-window and full-attention layers, and Gemma 3 uses five sliding-window layers (of 1,024 tokens) for each full one, so most layers have a small cache and a few still see everything.

Going deeper

Counting the work, with and without the cache

Split one decoder layer’s work into two kinds. The per-token work (the projections and the feed-forward network) costs about \(c\, d^2\) for every position it runs on. The attention work costs about the same for every (query, key) pair it scores and mixes.

Without the cache, step \(k\) reruns all \(k\) positions, and with the mask position \(i\) reads \(i\) keys, so the step scores \(1 + 2 + \cdots + k = k(k+1)/2\) pairs. Over \(n\) steps:

\[\text{positions: } \sum_{k=1}^{n} k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}, \qquad \text{pairs: } \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{k(k+1)}{2} = \frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6} \approx \frac{n^3}{6}\]

With the cache, step \(k\) runs one position, whose one query reads \(k\) keys:

\[\text{positions: } n, \qquad \text{pairs: } \sum_{k=1}^{n} k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} \approx \frac{n^2}{2}\]

The cache takes one power of \(n\) off both. Generation stays quadratic in total, but only through the attention term, which for short texts is the small one.

The cache is exact: the proof

Claim: after step \(t\), every layer’s key and value cache equals the keys and values a full masked pass over the first \(t\) tokens would compute. Use induction on \(t\).

  • Start. At \(t = 1\) there is one token, and the decode step computes exactly what the full pass computes.
  • Step. Suppose the claim holds after step \(t - 1\). The rows for positions \(1 \dots t-1\) are already right, and the full pass over \(t\) tokens leaves them unchanged, because the decoder is causal: appending a token can’t change earlier outputs. For the new row, go up the layers. Layer 1’s input at position \(t\) is the token’s embedding plus position, same in both. Its query attends over a cache that is right by assumption plus its own new key and value, so its output matches. That output is layer 2’s input at position \(t\), and so on to the top.

So the cache changes how much work is done, never the result. The figure’s “same answer” table checks this on your sentence.

Prefill and decode are different kinds of work

A GPU can do arithmetic far faster than it can read memory. An H100 does about 990 trillion 16-bit operations per second but reads about 3.35 trillion bytes per second: roughly 300 operations in the time it takes to read one byte.

  • Prefill pushes the whole prompt through at once. Every weight that is read gets used for hundreds or thousands of tokens, so the chip stays busy with arithmetic. This is compute-bound, like training.
  • Decode pushes one token per sequence. Every weight read from memory is used for one multiply-add per sequence, a couple of operations per two-byte number. The chip spends most of its time waiting for memory. This is memory-bound.

A rough count makes this precise. Multiplying a batch of \(B\) rows by a \(d \times d\) weight matrix takes \(2 B d^2\) operations (a multiply and an add for each pair) and reads the \(d^2\) weights once, \(2d^2\) bytes at 16 bits. That is

\[\frac{2 B d^2 \text{ operations}}{2 d^2 \text{ bytes}} = B \text{ operations per byte}\]

To keep an H100 busy it needs about 300. Prefill gets \(B\) = the number of prompt tokens, easily enough. A single decoding sequence gets \(B = 1\).

Serving many sequences at once (batching) helps decode, because they all share the weights: one read of \(W_Q\) serves the whole batch. The cache can’t be shared, though: every sequence reads its own. Do the same count for attention over the cache. One query head reads \(n\) cached keys and values of \(d_{head}\) numbers each, \(4 n\, d_{head}\) bytes, and does about \(4 n\, d_{head}\) operations with them: about 1 operation per byte, whatever the batch. With grouped-query attention, the \(g\) query heads in a group read the same cached keys and values, so the ratio rises to about \(g\). At long contexts reading the cache dominates, which is why shrinking it with GQA or MQA speeds up decoding, not just saves memory. Much of Pope et al. (2022) is this analysis, at scale.

Multi-head latent attention: cache something smaller

DeepSeek-V2 (2024) keeps 128 query heads and effectively 128 key/value heads, but caches neither keys nor values. Each token’s vector is first squeezed into a small latent vector,

\[c = x\, W_{down}, \qquad c \in \mathbb{R}^{512},\]

and that’s what gets cached. Each head’s keys and values are \(c\, W_{up}^{K}\) and \(c\, W_{up}^{V}\). Because matrix products can be regrouped, \(W_{up}^{K}\) can be folded into \(W_Q\) ahead of time (and \(W_{up}^{V}\) into \(W_O\)), so the full keys are never written out.

There’s one catch: RoPE (next section) rotates keys by position, and a rotation stuck between \(W_{up}^{K}\) and \(W_Q\) breaks the folding. So DeepSeek-V2 also caches one small 64-number key that carries the position. That’s 576 numbers per token per layer, against 32,768 for 128 full heads: 57 times smaller. The paper reports a 93% smaller cache than its previous 67B model.

Positions inside the cache

Our toy adds the sinusoidal position encoding to the input, as the paper does, so a cached key already “knows” its position. Most models today use rotary embeddings (RoPE) instead: rather than adding a position to the input, they rotate each query and key by an angle proportional to its position, inside every attention layer.

That works well with a cache. A key’s rotation depends only on its own position, so it’s rotated once and stored rotated. And part 2’s rotation trick does the rest: the score between a query at position \(p\) and a key at \(k\) depends only on the distance \(p - k\), however long the cache gets.

FlashAttention and the online softmax

The cache saves recomputation, but each step still reads every cached key and value. FlashAttention speeds up the attention computation itself by never writing the full score matrix to the GPU’s main memory: it reads \(K\) and \(V\) in blocks small enough for fast on-chip memory, and finishes each block before loading the next.

The hard part is the softmax, which seems to need every score before it can divide. The trick (Milakov & Gimelshein, 2018) is to keep a running maximum \(m\), a running sum \(\ell\) and a running output \(o\). For each new block of scores \(s_j\):

\[m' = \max(m,\, \max_j s_j)\] \[\ell' = e^{m - m'}\ell + \textstyle\sum_j e^{s_j - m'}\] \[o' = e^{m - m'}\, o + \textstyle\sum_j e^{s_j - m'}\, v_j\]

and the answer is \(o / \ell\) at the end. The factor \(e^{m - m'}\) rescales everything so far whenever a bigger score turns up.

Why is that right? After each block, three things stay true of the scores seen so far:

\[m = \max_j s_j, \qquad \ell = \sum_j e^{s_j - m}, \qquad o = \sum_j e^{s_j - m}\, v_j\]

The update keeps them true. Multiplying the old \(\ell\) by \(e^{m - m'}\) turns each \(e^{s_j - m}\) into \(e^{s_j - m'}\): the old terms, re-expressed against the new maximum. Then the new block’s terms are added in, against the same maximum. The same goes for \(o\). At the end, the common factor \(e^{-m}\) cancels:

\[\frac{o}{\ell} = \frac{\sum_j e^{s_j - m} v_j}{\sum_j e^{s_j - m}} = \sum_j \frac{e^{s_j}}{\sum_l e^{s_l}}\, v_j = \text{softmax}(s) \cdot V\]

And since \(m\) is the largest score so far, every exponent is at most 0, so nothing overflows. On the cached step in the figure above, done two keys at a time, it matches the direct softmax to about \(10^{-16}\), the last digit a computer keeps. FlashAttention is exact, not an approximation; it changes how much memory traffic attention needs, not what it computes.

PagedAttention: the cache as virtual memory

A server doesn’t know in advance how long each answer will be. Reserving a cache for the maximum length wastes most of it; vLLM found earlier systems used as little as a fifth of the memory they reserved. PagedAttention borrows the operating system’s answer: split the cache into small fixed-size blocks, hand them out as a sequence grows, and keep a table of where each sequence’s blocks are. Sequences that share a prompt can share its blocks. The authors report 2–4× more throughput at the same latency.

Speculative decoding: use part 4’s trick in reverse

Part 4 showed that one masked pass over a sentence gives the same predictions as writing it word by word. Speculative decoding uses that to break the one-word-per-pass limit. A small, fast model drafts a few words ahead. The big model then checks all of them in one pass, the way it would during training, and keeps the drafted words up to the first one it disagrees with, plus its own word at that point.

Every pass of the big model yields at least one word, and often several. With the right acceptance rule for sampling, the output follows exactly the big model’s distribution.

The rule is short. Let \(p\) be the big model’s probabilities for the next word and \(q\) the small model’s. The small model drafts a word \(x\) from \(q\). Accept it with probability \(\min(1,\ p(x)/q(x))\). If it’s rejected, draw a replacement from the leftover distribution

\[r(x) = \frac{\max(0,\ p(x) - q(x))}{\sum_y \max(0,\ p(y) - q(y))}\]

Proof that this samples from \(p\). Write \(\beta = \sum_y \min(p(y), q(y))\) for the overall chance of accepting. There are two ways to end up with word \(x\):

  • drafted and accepted: \(q(x) \cdot \min(1, p(x)/q(x)) = \min(p(x), q(x))\);
  • some draft rejected, then \(x\) drawn from \(r\): \((1 - \beta)\, r(x)\).

Since \(p(y) = \min(p(y), q(y)) + \max(0, p(y) - q(y))\) and \(p\) adds up to 1, the denominator of \(r\) is exactly \(1 - \beta\). So the second way has probability \(\max(0, p(x) - q(x))\), and the total is

\[\min(p(x), q(x)) + \max(0,\ p(x) - q(x)) = p(x)\]

The small model only changes how fast the words come out, not which words are likely. A good draft model (one with \(q\) close to \(p\)) just makes \(\beta\) big, so most drafts are kept. The authors report 2–3× faster decoding on T5-XXL with identical outputs.

How many words does one pass buy?

Leviathan et al. (2022) also work out the speed-up. Let the small model draft \(\gamma\) words, and call \(\alpha\) the average of \(\beta\), the chance that a draft is accepted. Assume, to keep it simple, that each draft is accepted independently with chance \(\alpha\).

Step 1: the words per pass. Let \(N\) be the number of words one big pass produces. If the first \(k\) drafts are accepted and draft \(k+1\) is rejected, we keep \(k\) drafts plus the big model’s replacement: \(N = k + 1\). If all \(\gamma\) are accepted, the big model’s pass has already computed the next word’s probabilities too, so we get a free extra word: \(N = \gamma + 1\). Either way, \(N \ge k + 1\) exactly when the first \(k\) drafts are accepted:

\[\Pr(N \ge k + 1) = \alpha^k, \qquad k = 0, 1, \dots, \gamma\]

Step 2: the average. For a count that is never negative, the average is the sum of the chances of being at least each value, \(\mathbb{E}[N] = \sum_{j \ge 1} \Pr(N \ge j)\). So

\[\mathbb{E}[N] = \sum_{k=0}^{\gamma} \alpha^k = \frac{1 - \alpha^{\gamma + 1}}{1 - \alpha}\]

the usual geometric sum. Even with endless drafts it can’t pass \(1/(1 - \alpha)\): 5 words per pass for \(\alpha = 0.8\).

Step 3: the cost. One round costs \(\gamma\) small-model steps plus one big pass. If a small step costs \(c\) times a big one, a round costs \(\gamma c + 1\) big passes. Plain decoding gets one word per big pass, so the speed-up is

\[\text{speed-up} = \frac{1 - \alpha^{\gamma+1}}{(1 - \alpha)(\gamma c + 1)}\]

With \(\gamma = 1\) this is \((1 + \alpha)/(1 + c)\), which is above 1 whenever \(\alpha > c\). So speculation always helps when the draft is accepted more often than it costs. For \(\alpha = 0.8\) and \(c = 0.05\):

drafts \(\gamma\) 1 2 3 5 8 10
words per pass \(\mathbb{E}[N]\) 1.80 2.44 2.95 3.69 4.33 4.57
speed-up 1.71 2.22 2.57 2.95 3.09 3.05

Past about 8 drafts, the extra drafting costs more than the words it adds. Two things the formula leaves out: the big model has to do more total arithmetic (it checks drafts that get thrown away), which only pays off because decoding is limited by memory reads, not arithmetic, as above; and real acceptances aren’t independent, so the table is a guide, not a promise.

Choosing the next word

Part 4 always took the most likely word (greedy). Chat models usually sample from the probabilities instead, after reshaping them:

  • Temperature \(T\) divides the logits before the softmax: \(\text{softmax}(z / T)\). Below 1 sharpens the distribution towards greedy; above 1 flattens it. It’s the √d_k story from part 1 again: dividing scores changes how peaked a softmax is.
  • Top-k keeps only the \(k\) most likely words and renormalises.
  • Top-p or nucleus sampling (Holtzman et al., 2019) keeps the smallest set of words whose probabilities add up to \(p\). It’s a fixed share of the probability rather than a fixed number of words, so it adapts: few candidates when the model is sure, many when it isn’t.

None of these change the cache: they act only on the final probabilities.

Further reading

  • Noam Shazeer, Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need (2019): multi-query attention, and a clear cost analysis of incremental decoding.
  • Ainslie et al., GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints (2023).
  • Pope et al., Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference (2022): prefill vs. decode, memory vs. compute, at scale.
  • Dao et al., FlashAttention (2022), and Kwon et al., PagedAttention (2023).
  • DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-V2 (2024), section 2.1: multi-head latent attention.
  • Leviathan, Kalman and Matias, Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding (2022): the acceptance rule and the speed-up formula.
  • kipply, Transformer Inference Arithmetic (2022): KV-cache sizes and the memory-vs-compute count, worked by hand.
