link.title: attention is all you need, part 4: the decoder, masking and training

entry.content:
Series · Attention is all you need 1Self-attention from scratch 2Multi-head attention and positions 3One encoder block 4The decoder, masking and training 5Inference and the KV cache

The first three parts built the encoder: it reads a sentence and turns each word into a vector shaped by the whole sentence. Part 3 ended with a stack of encoder blocks.

The paper’s Transformer was built for translation, so it also needs a way to write. That is the decoder, the right half of Figure 1. It reuses almost everything we’ve seen, with two changes:

  1. Its self-attention is masked, so a word can’t peek at the words that come after it.
  2. It adds cross-attention, where it reads the encoder’s output.

This part covers the decoder, the output layer, the loop that writes a sentence word by word, and how the whole thing is trained.

Our toy can’t translate: it has 35 words and has never been trained. So its task is the simplest one there is: copy the sentence. The encoder reads “the cat sat on the mat” and the decoder should write it back. The arithmetic is the same as for translation; only the training data would differ.

The decoder, step by step

Here are both halves. On the left, the encoder from part 3. On the right, the decoder.

A decoder block has three sublayers instead of two, each wrapped in Add & Norm:

  1. masked self-attention over the words written so far,
  2. cross-attention, which reads the encoder’s output (the blue line),
  3. the same kind of feed-forward network as the encoder.

Like the encoder, the paper stacks N = 6 of them. Everything outside the dashed frames runs once: the embeddings and positions at the bottom, and, at the top of the decoder, a linear layer and a softmax that turn the last vector into word probabilities. Notice the forks: self-attention takes Q, K and V from the line below, but cross-attention takes only Q from below. Its K and V arrive from the encoder.

How is the decoder trained? We already know the right output, so we feed it in, moved one place to the right, with a start token <s> in front.

Then every position has a simple job: predict the word under it. After <s> comes the; after the comes cat; and so on.

This is called teacher forcing. All positions are trained at the same time, in one pass, which is much faster than generating word by word.

There’s a catch. If position 2 can attend to position 3, it can simply read the answer. The model would learn to copy instead of to predict.

So before the softmax, we add a mask: \(-\infty\) to every score above the diagonal, 0 everywhere else.

\[\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\right) V\]

Since \(e^{-\infty} = 0\), those words get exactly zero weight. Each row is a word that can only see itself and the words before it, just like when the model writes for real. (Why not just zero them afterwards?)

The second sublayer looks across. It is ordinary multi-head attention with one difference: the queries come from the decoder, but the keys and values come from the encoder’s output.

\[\text{Attention}(Q_{\text{decoder}},\, K_{\text{encoder}},\, V_{\text{encoder}})\]

So each word the decoder is writing asks: which source words matter for me right now? In translation, this is where the model lines up chat with cat. Hover or tap a word on the left.

Our weights are random, so the lines here don’t mean anything yet. There’s no mask: the whole source sentence is known from the start.

From vectors back to words. The decoder’s last row is a vector of 8 numbers. To turn it into a word, we score it against every word in the vocabulary.

The paper does this with the embedding table itself: the logits are \(y\,E^\top\), a dot product with each word’s embedding. Reusing \(E\) saves weights and ties input and output words together.

A softmax turns the logits into probabilities. (My post on next-word prediction is all about this last step.)

After training, the decoder writes one word at a time. Start with <s>. Run the decoder, pick the likeliest word, append it, run again. Stop at the end token </s>.

The encoder runs once; the decoder runs once per word.

Here is our toy doing exactly that. Its output is nonsense, because it hasn’t learned anything. A trained model runs the very same loop and gets the copy right. Real systems usually pick with beam search (the paper uses a beam of 4) rather than always taking the top word.

Training measures how wrong the model is. At each position, compare the model’s probabilities with the right answer using cross-entropy:

\[\text{loss} = -\sum_{w} \text{target}(w) \cdot \log p(w)\]

The paper uses label smoothing with \(\epsilon = 0.1\). Instead of asking for 100% on the right word, the target is 90%, with the other 10% spread over every other word. The paper notes that this makes the model less sure of itself, which hurts one measure (perplexity) but improves the translations (BLEU).

Our untrained model gives mat almost nothing, so the loss is high. Training uses its gradient to nudge every weight, over and over, to bring it down.

How big should each nudge be? The paper uses the Adam optimiser with a learning rate that changes as training goes on:

\[\text{lr} = \frac{\min\!\left(s^{-0.5},\ s \cdot w^{-1.5}\right)}{\sqrt{d_{model}}}\]

where \(s\) is the training step and \(w = 4000\) is the number of warmup steps.

For the first 4000 steps it grows in a straight line. Big steps at the very start, when the weights are random, tend to blow training up. After that it shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{\text{step}}\), so the model settles down.

The base model trained for 100,000 steps, about 12 hours on 8 GPUs.

And that’s the whole model. Every box in the paper’s Figure 1 is something we’ve now computed by hand:

  • embeddings and positional encodings (parts 1 and 2),
  • scaled dot-product and multi-head attention (parts 1 and 2),
  • Add & Norm and the feed-forward network (part 3),
  • masking, cross-attention, the output layer and training (this part).

Putting it all together

Here’s the full model, in the order the data moves:

  1. Encoder. Embed the source words, add positions, and run \(N\) encoder blocks.
  2. Decoder. Embed the words written so far, add positions, and run \(N\) decoder blocks. Each one does masked self-attention, cross-attention to the encoder’s output, and a feed-forward network.
  3. Output. Multiply the last decoder vector by \(E^\top\) and take the softmax to get the next word.
  4. Training. Teacher forcing, cross-entropy with label smoothing, and Adam with warmup.

The paper’s base model has \(d_{model} = 512\), 8 heads, \(d_{ff} = 2048\) and \(N = 6\): about 65 million weights. Our toy has a few thousand. The arithmetic is the same.

What came next

The paper’s encoder–decoder design split into two families almost at once:

  • Encoder only, like BERT (2018): just the left stack, for understanding text.
  • Decoder only, like GPT (2018): just the right stack, without cross-attention. Masked self-attention and the generation loop from this post are, more or less, how today’s chat models write.

The core of every one of them is the equation from part 1.

Going deeper

Why −∞ before the softmax, and not 0 after?

Adding \(-\infty\) to a score makes its \(e^{x}\) exactly 0, so the softmax of a masked row is

\[p_j = \frac{e^{x_j}}{\sum_{l \le i} e^{x_l}} \quad (j \le i)\]

and \(p_j = 0\) for \(j > i\).

That is exactly a softmax over the allowed words only. The row still adds up to 1, and future words play no part in it.

Now try it the other way: take the normal softmax, then set the future weights to 0. The row no longer adds up to 1. Worse, the future scores were in the denominator, so the weights that are left still carry a trace of the future words. The model could learn to read that trace.

In real code the mask is usually a large negative number such as \(-10^9\) rather than true \(-\infty\). If a whole row is masked (it happens with padding), true infinities give \(0/0\), which is NaN. The causal mask always leaves the diagonal open, so our toy can use real \(-\infty\).

Why one masked pass equals writing word by word

Call a layer causal if its output at position \(i\) depends only on its inputs at positions \(0 \dots i\). Check each part of a decoder block:

  • Masked self-attention is causal: row \(i\) of the weights is zero beyond column \(i\), so output \(i\) mixes only values \(0 \dots i\).
  • Cross-attention reads the encoder’s output, which is fixed, plus the decoder’s row \(i\) alone. Causal.
  • Add & Norm and the feed-forward network work on each row on its own. Causal.

And a causal layer fed by a causal layer is causal: output \(i\) of the second depends on its inputs \(0 \dots i\), each of which depends only on positions up to itself. So by induction, layer after layer, the whole decoder is causal.

That’s the whole proof. Running the decoder on the full sentence at once gives each position exactly the vector it would get from the words up to that point alone. In our toy the two agree to the last digit.

That’s what makes teacher forcing work: one pass trains all \(n\) predictions at once. It also explains a trick every chat model uses when generating. Earlier positions never change, so their keys and values can be stored and reused (the KV cache). Each new word then costs one new row, rather than a rerun of the whole sentence. Part 5 draws it step by step.

Where the loss comes from

Training should make the right answer likely. The probability of a whole target sentence \(y_1 \dots y_n\), given the source \(x\), splits into one factor per word. This is just the chain rule of probability, true of any distribution:

\[p(y_1, \dots, y_n \mid x) = \prod_{t=1}^{n} p(y_t \mid y_1, \dots, y_{t-1},\, x)\]

Each factor is what position \(t - 1\) of the decoder predicts, and the mask guarantees it only sees \(y_1 \dots y_{t-1}\), exactly as the factor requires. Taking \(-\log\) turns the product into a sum:

\[-\log p(y \mid x) = \sum_{t=1}^{n} -\log p(y_t \mid y_{<t},\, x)\]

Each term is the cross-entropy of position \(t\) against a one-hot target. So minimising cross-entropy summed over positions is the same as maximising the likelihood of the training sentences.

The gradient is “prediction minus target”

Cross-entropy and softmax fit together unusually well. Write the logits as \(z\) and the probabilities as \(p = \text{softmax}(z)\), so \(\log p_w = z_w - \log \sum_v e^{z_v}\). For a target \(t\) that adds up to 1:

\[\text{loss} = -\sum_w t_w \log p_w = -\sum_w t_w z_w + \log \sum_v e^{z_v}\]

The derivative of the last term with respect to \(z_j\) is \(e^{z_j} / \sum_v e^{z_v} = p_j\). So

\[\frac{\partial\, \text{loss}}{\partial z_j} = p_j - t_j\]

No softmax Jacobian, no division: the gradient on each word’s logit is how much probability the model gave it minus how much it should have. Every learning signal in the model starts from this vector.

What label smoothing does to the loss

With a smoothed target \(t\), the loss \(-\sum_w t(w) \log p(w)\) is smallest when the model’s probabilities equal the target exactly, \(p = t\). Here is why. The cross-entropy splits into two parts:

\[-\sum_w t_w \log p_w = \underbrace{-\sum_w t_w \log t_w}_{H(t)} + \underbrace{\sum_w t_w \log \frac{t_w}{p_w}}_{\text{KL}(t \,\Vert\, p)}\]

The first part, the target’s entropy, doesn’t depend on the model at all. The second, the Kullback–Leibler divergence, is never negative and is 0 only when \(p = t\) (Gibbs’ inequality). So the loss can never go below \(H(t)\).

That floor is above 0 whenever the target is spread out. For the paper’s shared vocabulary of about 37,000 tokens that floor is about 1.38; for our 35 words it is 0.68.

So the best the model can do is put 90% on the right word, never 100%. The gradient says the same thing. With a one-hot target, the right word’s gradient is \(p - 1\), which is negative until \(p\) reaches exactly 1: the logit is pushed up forever, and the model is rewarded for becoming ever more certain. With smoothing, it is \(p - 0.9\), which turns positive once the model is more than 90% sure, and pushes back. Smoothing removes the reward for overconfidence. The paper reports that this makes the model less certain (worse perplexity) but improves both accuracy and BLEU.

Why warm up?

The paper doesn’t say. There are two common explanations, and they don’t exclude each other:

  • Adam needs data first. Adam divides each step by a running estimate of how big the gradients are. In the first few steps that estimate rests on very few samples, so some steps come out far too large. A small learning rate keeps those early steps safe (Liu et al., 2019).
  • Post-norm is touchy. With LayerNorm after each add, as in the paper, gradients near the output are large at the start of training. Moving the LayerNorm inside the residual branch (pre-norm) tames them, and such models can train without any warmup (Xiong et al., 2020).

Where is the peak? The schedule is the smaller of a falling curve, \(s^{-0.5}\), and a rising line, \(s \cdot w^{-1.5}\). They cross where

\[s^{-0.5} = s \cdot w^{-1.5} \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad s^{1.5} = w^{1.5} \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad s = w\]

so the switch from warming up to decaying happens exactly at step \(w\), and the peak learning rate is \(d_{model}^{-0.5} \cdot w^{-0.5}\).

For the record, the paper’s Adam settings were \(\beta_1 = 0.9\), \(\beta_2 = 0.98\), \(\epsilon = 10^{-9}\). The schedule peaks at step 4000, at \(512^{-0.5} \cdot 4000^{-0.5} \approx 7.0 \times 10^{-4}\).

Why Adam’s first steps are unreliable: the variance argument

Liu et al. (2019) turned the first explanation into a calculation. Adam scales each step by an adaptive factor \(\psi_t = 1 / \sqrt{\hat v_t}\), where \(\hat v_t\) is its running average of squared gradients. The question is how much that factor jumps around early on.

At step 1 its variance is infinite. The average holds one sample, so \(\hat v_1 = g_1^2\) and \(\psi_1 = 1/\lvert g_1 \rvert\). Model the gradient as random noise around 0, \(g_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\), with density \(\varphi\). Then

\[\mathbb{E}\big[\psi_1^2\big] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\varphi(g)}{g^2}\, dg\]

Near \(g = 0\) the density is about \(\varphi(0) > 0\), and \(\int_{-\delta}^{\delta} dg / g^2\) is infinite. So the expected square of \(\psi_1\) is infinite: a gradient that happens to be tiny makes the factor huge.

(A caveat: with bias correction, Adam’s actual first step is \(\hat m_1 / \sqrt{\hat v_1} = g_1 / \lvert g_1 \rvert\), just the sign of \(g_1\), which is bounded. The trouble is the factor \(\psi\) itself, which over the next steps multiplies a momentum built from different gradients than the ones in \(\hat v\).)

Later, it shrinks with the number of samples. An exponential average with decay \(\beta_2\) behaves roughly like a plain average of a limited number of samples. The paper calls that number \(\rho_t\):

\[\rho_\infty = \frac{2}{1 - \beta_2} - 1, \qquad \rho_t = \rho_\infty - \frac{2 t\, \beta_2^t}{1 - \beta_2^t}\]

Treating \(1/\hat v_t\) like a scaled chi-squared variable with \(\rho_t\) degrees of freedom, they get

\[\text{Var}[\psi_t] \approx \frac{\rho_t}{2(\rho_t - 2)(\rho_t - 4)\, \sigma^2}\]

which is finite only once \(\rho_t > 4\), and falls towards its final value as \(\rho_t\) grows. Their fix, RAdam, multiplies the step by \(r_t\), the square root of (final variance ÷ current variance), and uses plain momentum SGD while \(\rho_t \le 4\). For the paper’s \(\beta_2 = 0.98\), \(\rho_\infty = 99\), and:

\(t\) 1–4 5 10 50 100 500
\(\rho_t\) < 4 4.92 9.67 41.7 68.4 99.0
\(r_t\) – 0.08 0.22 0.62 0.82 1.00

(In steps 1–4 RAdam takes a plain momentum step instead.) That is a warmup, derived instead of hand-tuned: it ramps from almost 0 to full size over a few hundred steps. The paper’s 4000-step warmup is far longer, which is one hint that the post-norm explanation matters too.

One table for three jobs

The paper uses a single matrix for three jobs: the encoder’s input embedding, the decoder’s input embedding, and the final layer that turns vectors into word scores (Press & Wolf, 2016). With 37,000 tokens and \(d = 512\), each copy would be about 19 million weights, so sharing saves tens of millions.

It also makes sense: a word’s score is high when the decoder’s vector points the same way as that word’s embedding. The paper also multiplies the embeddings by \(\sqrt{d_{model}}\) on the way in. A common explanation: a table shared with the output layer starts with small numbers, and the scaling keeps the words from being drowned out by the positional encodings.

Can 512 numbers describe 37,000 choices?

The output layer has a hidden limit. Stack the decoder’s final vectors for many different contexts into a matrix \(H\) (one row per context, \(d\) columns) and the embedding table into \(E\) (one row per token). The scores are \(H E^\top\). A product through \(d\) columns has rank at most \(d\).

The model’s log-probabilities are the scores minus each row’s log-sum-exp:

\[\log P = H E^\top - c\, \mathbf{1}^\top, \qquad c_i = \log \sum_w e^{(H E^\top)_{iw}}\]

Subtracting \(c\,\mathbf{1}^\top\) is subtracting a rank-1 matrix, which raises the rank by at most 1. So every log-probability matrix the model can produce has rank at most \(d + 1\), however many contexts and tokens there are. Yang et al. (2017) call this the softmax bottleneck. If the true log-probabilities of language, over all contexts, have rank higher than \(d + 1\), then some contexts must get the wrong distribution, whatever the weights.

Whether language really is that high-rank can’t be proved, but they measured it. On a 10,000-token language-modelling task, the plain softmax’s log-probability matrix had rank about equal to \(d\) (400), as the bound says. Their mixture of softmaxes, which averages several softmaxes before taking the log, is not limited by it: its matrix reached rank 9,981, and its perplexity improved. For the paper’s \(d = 512\) and 37,000 tokens, the bound is real, though bigger \(d\) in later models makes it bite less.

Counting to 65 million

The weights of the base model (\(d = 512\), \(d_{ff} = 4d\), \(N = 6\), ignoring biases and LayerNorms) add up from the pieces of this series:

  • each encoder block: \(4d^2\) for attention and \(8d^2\) for the feed-forward network, so \(12 d^2\);
  • each decoder block: two attention sublayers and a feed-forward network, so \(16 d^2\);
  • the shared embedding table: \(37{,}000 \times 512\).
\[6 \cdot 12 d^2 + 6 \cdot 16 d^2 + 37{,}000\, d = 18.9\text{M} + 25.2\text{M} + 18.9\text{M} \approx 63\text{M}\]

That is close to the 65 million the paper reports (Table 3). Without the shared table it would be about 38 million more. Attention itself is under a third of the total; the feed-forward networks and the embeddings hold the rest.

Why teacher forcing, and not training on the model’s own words?

Teacher forcing feeds the decoder the right previous words, even where the model would have picked wrong ones. That has a cost, called exposure bias: in training the model never sees its own mistakes, so in use one bad word can lead it somewhere it has never been.

The alternative, feeding the model its own picks during training, would fix that, but it brings back the RNN’s problem. Each word would have to wait for the previous one to be chosen, so training would need \(n\) passes per sentence instead of one. Scheduled sampling mixes the two, but for Transformers the speed of teacher forcing has mostly won.

Greedy decoding vs. beam search

Our loop takes the single most likely word every time (greedy decoding). That can paint the model into a corner: a word that looks best now can lead to a worse sentence overall.

Beam search keeps the best few partial sentences at every step instead of one. The paper keeps 4. A sentence’s score is the sum of its words’ log-probabilities, which favours short outputs, since every extra word adds a negative number. A length penalty (\(\alpha = 0.6\) in the paper) corrects for that.

The penalty comes from Google’s translation system (Wu et al., 2016, eq. 14), which the paper cites. Divide the log-probability by a slowly growing function of the length \(\lvert Y \rvert\):

\[\text{score}(Y) = \frac{\log P(Y \mid X)}{\text{lp}(Y)}, \qquad \text{lp}(Y) = \left(\frac{5 + \lvert Y \rvert}{5 + 1}\right)^{\alpha}\]

With \(\alpha = 0\), \(\text{lp} = 1\) and nothing changes. With \(\alpha = 1\), it is close to dividing by the length: an average per word. \(\alpha = 0.6\) sits in between. The 5 keeps very short outputs from being divided by almost nothing, and the \(+1\) makes \(\text{lp} = 1\) for one word.

A worked case. A 3-token candidate with \(\log P = -3.0\) beats an 8-token one with \(\log P = -3.8\) on raw score. With the penalty:

\[\frac{-3.0}{(8/6)^{0.6}} = \frac{-3.0}{1.188} = -2.52, \qquad \frac{-3.8}{(13/6)^{0.6}} = \frac{-3.8}{1.590} = -2.39\]

Now the longer sentence wins. Google’s system also adds a coverage term, which rewards translations that attend to every source word; the Transformer paper reports only \(\alpha\). It also stops decoding at the input length plus 50 tokens.

Further reading

  • Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need, sections 3.1–3.4 (decoder and output) and 5 (training).
  • Harvard NLP, The Annotated Transformer: the full model and training loop in PyTorch, including the mask and label smoothing.
  • Andrej Karpathy, Let’s build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out: a decoder-only Transformer, built live.
  • Jay Alammar, The Illustrated GPT-2: the decoder-only family, in pictures.
  • Jay Mody, GPT in 60 Lines of NumPy (2023): a working decoder you can read in one sitting.
  • Liu et al., On the Variance of the Adaptive Learning Rate and Beyond (2019): the variance argument for warmup, and RAdam.
  • Yang et al., Breaking the Softmax Bottleneck (2017): the rank limit of the output layer.
  • Wu et al., Google’s Neural Machine Translation System (2016): where the length penalty comes from.

entry.content:
Series · Attention is all you need 1Self-attention from scratch 2Multi-head attention and positions 3One encoder block 4The decoder, masking and training 5Inference and the KV cache

Part 2 finished the multi-head attention sublayer. On its own it lets words share information, but a Transformer needs a few more parts around it to train well and to do something with that information.

Those parts make up one encoder block, the left half of the paper’s Figure 1. There are three new ideas, all small:

  1. Residual connections: add a sublayer’s input back to its output.
  2. Layer normalisation: rescale each word’s numbers to mean 0 and variance 1.
  3. A feed-forward network: two matrix multiplies with a ReLU between them, applied to each word on its own.

Same toy model as before, now with positions added. Edit the sentence and every matrix below recomputes.

Inside the block, step by step

Here is the whole block. Read it from the bottom up, the way the data flows.

At the bottom, each word is looked up in the embedding table and its positional encoding is added (the ⊕), giving \(X + PE\) from part 2. That happens once, outside the frame. The block itself starts where the line forks into three: the same input becomes the queries, keys and values of multi-head attention. Then comes Add & Norm, then a feed-forward network, then Add & Norm again.

The numbers under each box are the toy’s sizes, and the shape on the arrows (\(n \times 8\)) is the same in and out.

The lines running up the right side skip around each sublayer. They are the residual connections. The dashed frame with “× N” means the paper stacks N = 6 of these blocks.

The first “Add”. Take the block’s input X and the output of attention, and add them, number by number:

\[X + \text{MultiHead}(X)\]

This is a residual connection (from ResNet, 2015). Attention doesn’t have to rebuild each word’s vector from scratch. It only has to learn a change to add on top.

That makes deep stacks much easier to train (here’s why). If a block has nothing useful to add, it can learn to add almost nothing, and the word passes through unharmed.

Then “Norm”. For each word separately, compute the mean and variance of its 8 numbers. Subtract the mean and divide by the square root of the variance:

\[\text{LayerNorm}(x) = \gamma \cdot \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} + \beta\]

The number line underneath shows one row before and after. The dots keep their order and their relative spacing; they are just shifted and squeezed so the mean sits at 0 and the spread is 1. Hover or tap a word to see its row.

Without this, numbers can drift bigger and bigger as they pass through the layers. \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) are learned per column, so the model can undo the squeeze where it helps. Ours start at 1 and 0.

The second sublayer is a tiny neural network. First, multiply each word’s 8 numbers by \(W_1\), an 8 × 16 matrix. Every word grows to 16 numbers.

Then apply ReLU, which keeps positive numbers and turns negative ones into 0. Watch the hidden matrix: at the end of the step every blue (negative) cell turns grey: it is now 0.

This is the only non-linear step in the block apart from softmax. Without it, two matrix multiplies in a row would collapse into one.

Then multiply by \(W_2\), a 16 × 8 matrix, to get back to 8 numbers per word. Together that is the paper’s equation (2):

\[\text{FFN}(x) = \max(0,\, x W_1 + b_1)\, W_2 + b_2\]

Notice what this step doesn’t do: it never mixes rows. Every word goes through the same two matrices on its own. The paper calls it position-wise. Attention moves information between words; the feed-forward network works on what each word has gathered.

In the paper the hidden layer has 2048 numbers per word, against 512 for the model. That makes the feed-forward network about two thirds of each block’s weights.

The same trick a second time. Add the feed-forward network’s input to its output, then apply LayerNorm:

\[\text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{FFN}(x))\]

The result is the block’s output. It has exactly the same shape as the input: one row of 8 numbers per word.

Same shape in, same shape out. That means the output of one block can be fed straight into the next.

Each block has its own weights, so each one can refine the vectors a bit more. Our toy uses 2 blocks; the paper uses N = 6, and large modern models use 100 or more.

The output of the last block is the encoder’s final answer: one vector per word, each one shaped by the whole sentence. In part 4 the decoder reads it.

The whole block in two lines

Writing \(x\) for the input of a block, the paper’s encoder layer is:

\[h = \text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{MultiHead}(x))\] \[\text{out} = \text{LayerNorm}(h + \text{FFN}(h))\]

All sublayers, and the embeddings too, produce \(d_{model} = 512\) numbers per word in the paper (8 in our toy), precisely so these additions line up.

Two details from the paper I left out of the figure. Dropout is applied to each sublayer’s output before the add, with rate 0.1 in training. And the order shown here, add first and then normalise (“post-norm”), is the original. Most models today normalise first, \(x + \text{Sublayer}(\text{LayerNorm}(x))\) (“pre-norm”), because it trains more stably in deep stacks.

Going deeper

Why residual connections help learning

Training works backwards. The loss sends a gradient back through every layer, and each layer multiplies it by its own derivative. With a residual connection, a sublayer computes \(y = x + F(x)\), so its derivative is

\[\frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = I + \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}\]

The \(I\) (the identity) is the important part. Going back through \(N\) blocks multiplies \(N\) of these together. Multiply out the brackets and one of the terms is just \(I \cdot I \cdots I\): a path where the gradient reaches the first block untouched, however deep the stack.

Write it out for three blocks, with \(J_l = \partial F_l / \partial x\):

\[(I + J_3)(I + J_2)(I + J_1) = I + (J_1 + J_2 + J_3) + (J_2 J_1 + J_3 J_1 + J_3 J_2) + J_3 J_2 J_1\]

There is one term for every subset of blocks: \(2^N\) paths in all, of every length from 0 to \(N\). Most of them are short, and the shortest is the identity.

Without the skip, the gradient is a product of \(N\) derivatives \(\partial F / \partial x\): only the last, longest term. Products of many factors tend to shrink towards zero or blow up, which is why very deep networks were so hard to train before ResNet. Veit et al. (2016) give another way to see it: a residual network behaves like many shallow networks of different depths, added together.

Post-norm and pre-norm, unrolled

The algebra above assumes the add is the last thing a block does. In the paper’s post-norm block it isn’t: \(x_{l+1} = \text{LN}(x_l + F_l(x_l))\). Every path back to the input now passes through all \(N\) LayerNorms, and each one rescales the gradient by its own \(1/\sigma\) (see below). There is no clean identity path any more.

Pre-norm moves the norm inside the branch: \(x_{l+1} = x_l + F_l(\text{LN}(x_l))\). Unroll it and the input survives untouched to the top:

\[x_N = x_0 + \sum_{l=0}^{N-1} F_l\big(\text{LN}(x_l)\big)\]

Each block only adds to a running sum, often called the residual stream, and the gradient with respect to \(x_0\) always contains a plain \(I\). That is why deep pre-norm stacks train more easily, and why Xiong et al. (2020) found they don’t need the learning-rate warmup of part 4. The cost: since nothing rescales the sum, it grows as blocks pile on, so pre-norm models add one last LayerNorm before the output layer.

Attention alone collapses: why the skips are not optional

Residuals do more than help gradients. Without them, a stack of attention layers destroys its own input. Dong, Cordonnier and Loukas (2021) proved this; here is the core of the argument, then their result.

Take attention with no skip and no feed-forward network: \(X_{l+1} = P_l\, X_l\, W_V\), where each row of \(P_l\) is positive and adds up to 1. Pick one column \(v\) of \(X\) (one feature, across all \(n\) words) and measure how spread out it is by its range, \(\max_i v_i - \min_i v_i\).

Claim. If every entry of \(P\) is at least \(\varepsilon\), then \(\text{range}(Pv) \le (1 - n\varepsilon)\, \text{range}(v)\).

Proof. Compare two rows \(i\) and \(j\) of the output:

\[(Pv)_i - (Pv)_j = \sum_k a_k\, v_k, \qquad a_k = P_{ik} - P_{jk}\]

Both rows add up to 1, so \(\sum_k a_k = 0\): the positive \(a_k\) add up to some \(s\) and the negative ones to \(-s\). The sum is largest when all the positive weight sits on the biggest \(v_k\) and all the negative weight on the smallest, so

\[\sum_k a_k v_k \le s \max_k v_k - s \min_k v_k = s \cdot \text{range}(v)\]

And \(s\) is small. Each positive part is \(P_{ik} - \min(P_{ik}, P_{jk})\), so

\[s = \sum_k P_{ik} - \sum_k \min(P_{ik}, P_{jk}) = 1 - \sum_k \min(P_{ik}, P_{jk}) \le 1 - n\varepsilon\]

since each of the \(n\) minimums is at least \(\varepsilon\). This holds for every pair \(i, j\), which proves the claim. \(\blacksquare\)

So each attention layer pulls every feature closer to “the same for all words”. Repeat it and the rows of \(X\) converge to one shared row: \(X \to \mathbf{1} x^\top\), a matrix of rank 1, where every word holds the same vector. Softmax makes every weight strictly positive, so this always happens to some degree. The claim ignores \(W_V\), which mixes features and can stretch them back out. Dong et al. handle \(W_V\) and multiple heads too: measuring the distance from rank 1 by \(\text{res}(X) = X - \mathbf{1}x^\top\) (for the best \(x\)), they show it shrinks doubly exponentially with depth, with an exponent like \(3^L\). That is an upper bound, for a stack where the residual is already small; it says collapse can be very fast, not that it always is.

What saves real Transformers.

  • Skips. With \(X_{l+1} = X_l + P_l X_l W_V\), the same unrolling as in the residual section gives one path per subset of layers: \(\binom{L}{k} H^k\) paths through \(k\) of \(L\) layers with \(H\) heads, which is \(2^L\) for one head. The path through no attention at all is \(X_0\) itself, which never collapses. The paper shows that some settings of the weights then avoid collapse (the trivial one is \(W_V = 0\)); it is a guarantee that escape is possible, not that training finds it.
  • Feed-forward networks. They can pull rows apart again. The paper bounds how much by the network’s Lipschitz constant (how much it can stretch distances): the bigger it is, the slower the collapse.
  • Not LayerNorm. LayerNorm treats every row the same way, on its own. If all rows are already equal, they come out equal. It can’t split words that attention has merged.

What LayerNorm ignores

Ignoring the tiny \(\epsilon\), LayerNorm doesn’t change if you scale a row by any \(a > 0\) or shift all its numbers by the same \(c\). The mean of \(a x + c\) is \(a\mu + c\) and its standard deviation is \(a\sigma\), so

\[\frac{(a x + c) - (a\mu + c)}{a \sigma} = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\]

Before \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\), every output row \(z\) also has a fixed shape: its numbers add up to 0 (mean 0) and their squares add up to \(d\) (variance 1). So every row sits on the same sphere, of radius \(\sqrt{d}\). Whatever a sublayer does to the size of a word’s vector, the next one sees a vector of the same length.

The LayerNorm gradient

For one row \(x\) of \(d\) numbers with \(z = (x - \mu)/\sigma\), the derivative of the output with respect to the input is

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \frac{1}{\sigma}\left(I - \tfrac{1}{d}\,\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top - \tfrac{1}{d}\, z z^\top\right)\]

where \(\mathbf{1}\) is a row of ones. To see it, differentiate the two statistics: \(\partial \mu / \partial x_j = 1/d\) and \(\partial \sigma / \partial x_j = z_j / d\). Then the quotient rule on \(z_i = (x_i - \mu)/\sigma\) gives

\[\frac{\partial z_i}{\partial x_j} = \frac{\delta_{ij} - 1/d}{\sigma} - \frac{(x_i - \mu)}{\sigma^2}\cdot\frac{z_j}{d} = \frac{1}{\sigma}\left(\delta_{ij} - \frac{1}{d} - \frac{z_i z_j}{d}\right)\]

Read the bracket as an instruction: take the incoming gradient and remove the part along \(\mathbf{1}\) (shifting every number at once) and the part along \(z\) (scaling the row), since LayerNorm ignores both. Then divide by \(\sigma\). A row with a big spread gets a small gradient, which is the \(1/\sigma\) that post-norm stacks multiply together.

Why LayerNorm and not BatchNorm?

BatchNorm, common in image models, normalises each feature across all the examples in a batch. LayerNorm normalises each word across its own features. For text, LayerNorm is the better fit:

  • Sentences in a batch have different lengths and are padded. Batch statistics would mix in padding and depend on which other sentences happen to share the batch.
  • When generating, there is often only one sentence, so there is no batch to average over.
  • LayerNorm treats every word on its own, so it computes exactly the same thing in training and in use.

Why not RMSNorm?

Many recent models (Llama among them) use RMSNorm (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019), which skips the mean:

\[\text{RMSNorm}(x) = \gamma \cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{d}\sum_i x_i^2 + \epsilon}}\]

It keeps the scale invariance above and drops the shift invariance. The authors’ argument is that the rescaling is what does the work, and they found it matched LayerNorm’s quality while running faster, since there is one statistic to compute instead of two. The paper’s choice simply predates it.

Where the weights live

Count the weights in one block of the paper’s base model (\(d = 512\), \(d_{ff} = 2048\), ignoring the small biases and LayerNorm parameters):

  • attention: \(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O\) are 4 matrices of \(d \times d\), so \(4d^2 \approx 1.05\) million.
  • feed-forward: \(W_1\) is \(d \times 4d\) and \(W_2\) is \(4d \times d\), so \(8d^2 \approx 2.1\) million.

The feed-forward network holds two thirds of each block’s weights, and does most of its arithmetic too.

Why the ReLU is needed

Remove it and the network is two matrix multiplies in a row. Matrix products can be regrouped:

\[(x W_1) W_2 = x\, (W_1 W_2)\]

So the pair is just one \(d \times d\) matrix, \(W_1 W_2\), and the 2048 hidden numbers bought nothing. ReLU breaks the regrouping: \(\max(0, xW_1)\, W_2\) can’t be written as \(x\) times anything fixed, because which hidden units are switched on depends on \(x\).

Why widen to \(4d\) in the middle? A network with one hidden layer can approximate any reasonable function given enough hidden units, and each unit is one more pattern it can detect (see below). The width is a budget. The paper doesn’t explain the factor 4; most later models kept it, or something close.

Why ReLU, and not GELU or SwiGLU?

ReLU was the standard choice in 2017. Two smoother options came after:

  • GELU (Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016), used by BERT and GPT-2, is \(x \cdot \Phi(x)\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal’s cumulative probability. It bends smoothly near 0 instead of having a corner, and lets small negative numbers through.
  • SwiGLU (Shazeer, 2020), used by Llama and many others, adds a gate: a second matrix \(W_3\) whose output multiplies the hidden layer entry by entry,
\[\text{FFN}(x) = \big(\text{Swish}(x W_1) \odot x W_3\big)\, W_2\]

The gate lets one projection decide how much of the other gets through. Three matrices instead of two would cost more weights, so the hidden size is cut from \(4d\) to about \(\tfrac{2}{3} \cdot 4d\) to keep the total the same. Shazeer found the gated versions trained to a lower loss than ReLU at equal cost, and offered no deeper reason: “we attribute their success, as all else, to divine benevolence”.

What does the feed-forward network do?

Read equation (2) one hidden unit at a time. Each of the 2048 hidden units has a column of \(W_1\), which works like a key: its dot product with the word’s vector says how well the word matches some pattern. ReLU keeps only positive matches. The matching row of \(W_2\) is a value, added to the output in proportion to the match.

So the network is a big, fixed lookup: “if the word looks like this, add that”. Geva et al. (2021) found exactly this in trained models. In lower layers, keys tend to fire on surface patterns, such as text ending in a particular word; in higher layers, on topics. In the higher layers, the values push towards likely next words. It looks like attention, except the keys and values are learned once, rather than coming from the sentence.

Further reading

  • Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need, sections 3.1 (encoder stack) and 3.3 (feed-forward networks).
  • Ba, Kiros and Hinton, Layer Normalization (2016).
  • He et al., Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition (2015): where residual connections come from.
  • Xiong et al., On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture (2020): post-norm vs. pre-norm.
  • Dong, Cordonnier and Loukas, Attention is Not All You Need: Pure Attention Loses Rank Doubly Exponentially with Depth (2021): the rank-collapse result and why skips stop it.

entry.content:
Series · Attention is all you need 1Self-attention from scratch 2Multi-head attention and positions 3One encoder block 4The decoder, masking and training 5Inference and the KV cache

Part 1 built one attention head from scratch. It ended with two problems:

  1. Attention can’t tell word order. “The cat sat on the mat” and “mat the on sat cat the” look the same to it.
  2. One head can only ask one kind of question at a time.

The paper solves the first with positional encodings and the second with multi-head attention. Both are small ideas. Let’s see them with real numbers.

As before, this is the tiny model from part 1: 8 numbers per word and real arithmetic. The sentence is editable, and scrolling inside a step plays it.

Positions and heads, step by step

First, the problem. On the left is the output of an attention layer for our sentence. On the right is the same sentence reversed.

Every line joins a word to the same word in the other sentence. Their rows are exactly equal. The layer has no idea the order changed. It only moved the rows around.

That makes sense. Attention compares every word with every other word, and nothing in those comparisons says where a word is.

The fix: give each position its own fingerprint. The paper uses waves. Column \(2i\) of the encoding is a sine wave and column \(2i+1\) is a cosine, each at its own speed:

\[PE_{(pos,\,2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)\] \[PE_{(pos,\,2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)\]

The first pair of waves wiggles fast and the last pair barely moves. Read down at any position (the blue line) and you get 8 heights. That is the position’s row of PE. No two positions have the same row.

Then we simply add. Each word’s row of X gets its position’s row of PE added to it, number by number.

Adding, not appending, keeps the size at 8 numbers. The word is still in there, and now the position is too. Two copies of the at positions 0 and 4 now get different rows.

From here on, every layer sees \(X + PE\) instead of X.

Run the same test again, this time with positions added.

Now the lines turn red and dashed: the same word gets a different output depending on where it stands. Word order finally matters.

(There is nothing special about reversing. Any other order would show the same thing.)

Why waves, and not just the numbers 0, 1, 2, …? Plain counting grows without limit, and the network would only ever see small numbers while training.

Waves stay between −1 and 1. They also have a nice property. Treat each sine/cosine pair as a point on a circle. Moving one position later turns the point by the same angle, wherever it starts.

So “the word just before me” is the same rotation at position 3 as at position 300. A weight matrix can learn to recognise it once and use it everywhere. (The proof is below.) The paper says the authors chose waves because they hoped the model could “easily learn to attend by relative positions”.

Now the second problem. sat wants to know who sat, but also where. One softmax row can’t put most of its weight on two places at once.

So the Transformer runs several heads side by side. Each head has its own \(W_Q\), \(W_K\) and \(W_V\) and runs its own attention, exactly as in part 1.

Our toy has 2 heads. Head 1 is the hand-wired one from part 1. Head 2 is random. Hover or tap a row to compare them. In a trained model every head learns a pattern of its own. Some track the previous word, some link a pronoun to its noun, and some just look at punctuation.

Each head is made smaller, so the total cost stays the same. With \(d_{model} = 8\) and 2 heads, each head works with \(d_k = 8 / 2 = 4\) numbers.

The heads’ outputs are placed side by side (“concatenated”) to get back to 8 numbers per word. Then one more matrix, \(W_O\), mixes them. The square brackets mean “side by side”:

\[\text{MultiHead}(X) = [\,\text{head}_1 \cdots \text{head}_h\,]\, W_O\]

The paper uses 8 heads of 64 numbers each: \(8 \times 64 = 512 = d_{model}\).

Was it worth it? The paper compares attention with recurrent layers. Drag the slider to change the number of words.

Attention compares every pair of words, so its work grows like \(n^2\). A recurrent layer does less work per word for long inputs, but it has to go one word after another: \(n\) steps, each waiting for the last.

For sentences shorter than \(d\) (512 in the paper), attention is both cheaper and fully parallel. That speed is a big part of why Transformers took over. The \(n^2\) cost for very long texts is why so much later research tries to make attention cheaper.

What we have so far

We now have the full multi-head attention sublayer of the paper:

  1. Add positions: \(X \leftarrow X + PE\).
  2. For each head h: \(\text{head}_h = \text{Attention}(X W_Q^h,\; X W_K^h,\; X W_V^h)\).
  3. Join the heads and mix: \(\text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_h)\, W_O\).

Its output has the same shape as its input: one row of \(d_{model}\) numbers per word. The paper draws it as its Figure 2 (right). Drag the slider to change the number of heads, with the paper’s \(d_{model} = 512\):

One detail I glossed over: the paper also multiplies the embeddings by \(\sqrt{d_{model}}\) before adding positions, so the two have similar sizes. In this toy the embeddings already have about the right size, so I left that out.

Attention lets words share information, but it doesn’t do much with that information on its own. In part 3 we wrap it in the rest of an encoder block: residual connections, layer normalisation and a small feed-forward network.

Going deeper

Why a shift is a rotation

Take one sine/cosine pair with speed \(\omega\). Write \(a = \omega p\) for the angle at position \(p\), and \(b = \omega k\) for the extra angle after \(k\) more steps. The angle-addition rules say:

\[\sin(a + b) = \sin a \cos b + \cos a \sin b\] \[\cos(a + b) = \cos a \cos b - \sin a \sin b\]

In matrix form:

\[\begin{pmatrix} \sin(a+b) \\ \cos(a+b) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos b & \sin b \\ -\sin b & \cos b \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \sin a \\ \cos a \end{pmatrix}\]

The matrix in the middle is a rotation by the angle \(b = \omega k\). It depends on \(k\) but not on \(p\). So “\(k\) places later” is the same fixed matrix at every position. A weight matrix like \(W_Q\) multiplies by fixed matrices, so in principle it can learn “the word just before me” once and have it work everywhere.

Dot products only see distance

Here’s another consequence. Take the dot product of two position rows, \(PE(p)\) and \(PE(p+k)\). Each sine/cosine pair contributes \(\sin a \sin b + \cos a \cos b = \cos(a - b)\), so

\[PE(p) \cdot PE(p+k) = \sum_i \cos(\omega_i k)\]

This depends only on the distance \(k\), not on where you are. In our toy (\(d = 8\)), positions 3 apart always have a dot product of 1.96, whether they are positions 0 and 3 or 40 and 43.

It’s also the same for \(+k\) and \(-k\), since cosine doesn’t care about sign. On their own, the dot products can’t tell “3 words before” from “3 words after”. The rotation above can, which is one reason the learned \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\) matter.

Why add the positions, and not append them?

Appending would give each word \([x,\ p]\): twice as many numbers. But the first thing the layer does is multiply by a matrix. Split that matrix into a top half \(W_a\) (for the word) and a bottom half \(W_b\) (for the position):

\[[x,\ p] \begin{pmatrix} W_a \\ W_b \end{pmatrix} = x W_a + p W_b\]

So appending and then multiplying is the same as adding a transformed position. Adding the position directly is the special case \(W_b = W_a\), and it saves the extra width. In 512 dimensions there is plenty of room for the model to keep word and position information in different directions, so little is lost.

What a score sees once positions are added

With positions added, the score between word \(i\) and word \(j\) is \((x_i + p_i)\, A\, (x_j + p_j)^\top\), where \(A = W_Q W_K^\top\) as in part 1. Multiply out the brackets:

\[\underbrace{x_i A x_j^\top}_{\text{word–word}} + \underbrace{x_i A p_j^\top}_{\text{word–position}} + \underbrace{p_i A x_j^\top}_{\text{position–word}} + \underbrace{p_i A p_j^\top}_{\text{position–position}}\]

Each term asks a different question. The first is the content match from part 1. The last depends only on the two positions: “look one word back” lives here. The middle two mix the two: “the word at the start of the sentence”. One matrix \(A\) has to serve all four. Transformer-XL took this expansion as its starting point, and gave the position terms their own weights, using only the distance \(i - j\).

Why 10000, and why so many speeds?

The speeds are \(\omega_i = 1 / 10000^{2i/d}\), so the wavelengths grow geometrically from \(2\pi\) (about 6 positions) to \(10000 \cdot 2\pi\) (about 63,000 positions).

Think of the hands of a clock. The fast hand tells neighbouring positions apart, but it repeats every few steps. The slow hands barely move between neighbours, but they tell far-apart positions apart. Together, every position gets a unique pattern, and 10000 makes the slowest wave far longer than any sentence the model will see.

Learned positions work too

The paper also tried simply learning a vector for each position, like a second embedding table. The results were nearly identical (Table 3, row E). The authors kept the waves because they hoped the model could then handle sentences longer than any it saw in training.

Later models went both ways. BERT and GPT-2 learned their positions. Many of today’s models use RoPE (Su et al., 2021), which takes the rotation above literally: it rotates each query and key by its position, so a score depends only on the distance between the two words.

RoPE in one line

RoPE rotates the query of the word at position \(m\) by \(R_m\) (a rotation by \(m\omega\), as above) and the key at position \(n\) by \(R_n\). Their score is

\[(q R_m)\cdot(k R_n) = q\, R_m R_n^\top\, k^\top = q\, R_{m-n}\, k^\top\]

using two facts about rotations: undoing a rotation is rotating backwards (\(R_n^\top = R_{-n}\)), and two rotations add their angles (\(R_m R_{-n} = R_{m-n}\)). Only the distance \(m - n\) is left. Unlike the added waves, nothing about the absolute position survives in the score, and unlike plain dot products of positions, \(R_{m-n}\) and \(R_{n-m}\) differ, so before and after are told apart.

Deriving RoPE from what we want

The line above checks that rotation works. Su et al. (2021, section 3.4) go the other way: they start from the property we want and show that rotation is the answer. Here is that argument for one pair of numbers.

Set up. Treat a 2-number vector \((a, b)\) as the complex number \(a + ib\), where \(i = \sqrt{-1}\) (so in this section and the next, \(i\) is never an index). Then the dot product of two such vectors is the real part of one times the conjugate of the other: \((a, b) \cdot (c, d) = \text{Re}\big[(a + ib)(c - id)\big]\). We look for a way \(f(q, m)\) to mark a query \(q\) with its position \(m\) (and the same \(f\) for keys), such that

\[f(q, m)\; \overline{f(k, n)} = g(q, k, m - n) \qquad \text{and} \qquad f(x, 0) = x\]

The first condition says the product, and so the score, depends on the positions only through their distance. The second says position 0 leaves a vector alone.

Step 1: polar form. Write each complex number as a length and an angle: \(f(q, m) = r(q, m)\, e^{i \Theta(q, m)}\). Multiplying complex numbers multiplies lengths and adds angles (the conjugate flips the sign of an angle), so the condition splits in two:

\[r(q, m)\, r(k, n) = r_g(q, k, m - n), \qquad \Theta(q, m) - \Theta(k, n) = \Theta_g(q, k, m - n)\]

Step 2: lengths don’t move. Set \(n = m\), so the distance is 0. The right side no longer depends on \(m\), so it equals its value at \(m = 0\), where \(f(x, 0) = x\):

\[r(q, m)\, r(k, m) = r(q, 0)\, r(k, 0) = \lVert q\rVert\, \lVert k\rVert\]

The simplest solution, and the one RoPE uses, is \(r(q, m) = \lVert q \rVert\): marking a vector with its position never changes its length.

Step 3: every vector turns by the same amount. Do the same with the angles. Let \(\theta_q\) and \(\theta_k\) be the original angles of \(q\) and \(k\). With \(n = m\),

\[\Theta(q, m) - \Theta(k, m) = \theta_q - \theta_k \quad\Rightarrow\quad \Theta(q, m) - \theta_q = \Theta(k, m) - \theta_k\]

The left side involves only \(q\) and the right only \(k\), and they are equal for every \(q\) and \(k\). So both are some function of the position alone. Call it \(\phi(m)\): each vector is turned by \(\phi(m)\) at position \(m\), whatever it is.

Step 4: the turn grows in equal steps. Now set \(n = m - 1\), a distance of 1. The angle condition becomes

\[\big(\theta_q + \phi(m)\big) - \big(\theta_k + \phi(m-1)\big) = \Theta_g(q, k, 1)\]

so \(\phi(m) - \phi(m-1) = \Theta_g(q, k, 1) - \theta_q + \theta_k\), which does not depend on \(m\). A function that goes up by the same amount \(\omega\) at every step is a straight line, \(\phi(m) = m\omega + \phi(0)\), and \(f(x, 0) = x\) forces \(\phi(0) = 0\).

Result. Putting the length and the angle back together:

\[f(q, m) = \lVert q \rVert\, e^{i(\theta_q + m\omega)} = q\, e^{i m \omega}\]

Multiplying by \(e^{im\omega}\) is rotating by \(m\omega\). So once we ask for “distance only” and “position 0 does nothing” (plus the simple choice of length in step 2), rotation is the only answer. With \(d\) numbers, RoPE does this for each of the \(d/2\) pairs, with speeds \(\omega_l = 10000^{-2l/d}\), the same as the sinusoidal waves. The EleutherAI write-up walks through the same steps with code.

Do far-apart words matter less under RoPE?

Write the score as a sum over the \(d/2\) pairs. With \(h_l = q_{[l]}\, \overline{k_{[l]}}\) for pair \(l\) (as complex numbers) and distance \(r = m - n\):

\[\text{score} = \text{Re} \sum_{l=0}^{d/2 - 1} h_l\, e^{i r \omega_l}\]

Su et al. bound this with Abel summation, the sum version of integration by parts. Let \(S_0 = 0\) and \(S_j = \sum_{l < j} e^{i r \omega_l}\), so \(e^{i r \omega_l} = S_{l+1} - S_l\), and set \(h_{d/2} = 0\). Then, regrouping the terms,

\[\sum_l h_l (S_{l+1} - S_l) = -\sum_{j=1}^{d/2} S_j\, (h_j - h_{j-1}) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \lvert \text{score} \rvert \le \Big(\max_j \lvert h_j - h_{j-1} \rvert\Big) \sum_{j=1}^{d/2} \lvert S_j \rvert\]

The first factor depends only on \(q\) and \(k\). The second depends only on the distance \(r\), so it is a ceiling on how much any pair of vectors can score at that distance. For \(d = 128\), the average of \(\lvert S_j \rvert\) comes out at:

distance \(r\) 0 10 100 1000 4000
average \(\lvert S_j \rvert\) 32.5 18.0 10.2 4.5 5.0

The ceiling trends down as words get further apart, with some wiggles. Two caveats keep this honest. The decay is computed, not proved: the paper shows the same curve as a plot. And it is a bound for all possible \(q\) and \(k\), often far above the real score; a trained head can still look a thousand words back if its query and key line up.

Why one head can’t look at two places

Row \(i\) of a head’s weights is a set of positive numbers adding up to 1, so the output for word \(i\) is a weighted average of the value rows:

\[o_i = \sum_j P_{ij}\, v_j, \qquad P_{ij} \ge 0, \quad \sum_j P_{ij} = 1\]

Suppose sat needs both cat’s value and mat’s. The best one head can do is split its weight, say \(\lambda\) and \(1 - \lambda\), and return the blend \(\lambda v_{cat} + (1-\lambda) v_{mat}\). Both are in there, but mixed into the same numbers, and the more it gets of one, the less it gets of the other.

Two heads don’t have to share. Head 1 puts all its weight on cat, head 2 on mat, and the concatenation keeps the two values in separate columns. The next matrix, \(W_O\), sees each one whole.

Concat, then W_O, is a sum over heads

Cut \(W_O\) into \(h\) horizontal slices, one per head, each \(d_k \times d_{model}\). Multiplying a row of blocks by a column of blocks works block by block, so

\[[\,\text{head}_1 \cdots \text{head}_h\,] \begin{pmatrix} W_O^{(1)} \\ \vdots \\ W_O^{(h)} \end{pmatrix} = \sum_{k=1}^{h} \text{head}_k\, W_O^{(k)}\]

So “concatenate and mix” is the same as letting every head write its own contribution, through its own matrix, and adding them up. Nothing in the layer makes heads talk to each other. That is what lets researchers study one head at a time (Elhage et al., 2021).

Where the paper’s Table 1 comes from

The paper’s case for attention (section 4) is a table comparing layer types, for \(n\) words of \(d\) numbers each. Each entry is a count you can do by hand:

layer work per layer steps that must wait longest path between two words
self-attention \(O(n^2 d)\) \(O(1)\) \(O(1)\)
recurrent \(O(n d^2)\) \(O(n)\) \(O(n)\)
convolution, width \(k\) \(O(k\, n\, d^2)\) \(O(1)\) \(O(\log_k n)\)
  • Self-attention. \(QK^\top\) is \(n^2\) dot products of length \(d\). All of them are independent, so nothing waits. Every word reads every word directly, so any two are one step apart.
  • Recurrent. Each step computes \(h_t = f(h_{t-1} W + x_t U)\): a \(d \times d\) matrix times a vector, \(d^2\) work, done \(n\) times. Step \(t\) needs step \(t-1\), so there are \(n\) waits. Information from word 1 reaches word \(n\) after \(n\) steps.
  • Convolution. Each output reads \(k\) neighbours through a \(d \times d\) matrix each: \(k d^2\) per word. One layer only reaches \(k\) words, so joining two far-apart words takes a stack: \(O(n/k)\) layers, or \(O(\log_k n)\) with dilated convolutions.

Compare the first two: attention is cheaper exactly when \(n^2 d < n d^2\), that is when \(n < d\). With \(d = 512\), that held for most sentences in 2017. The last column is the deeper argument. A short path means a gradient from one word reaches another in one hop, which the paper argues makes long-range patterns easier to learn.

Many heads cost the same as one

Each head has its own \(W_Q\), \(W_K\) and \(W_V\), each of size \(d \times (d/h)\). Over \(h\) heads that is \(3 \cdot h \cdot d \cdot (d/h) = 3d^2\) weights, plus \(d^2\) for \(W_O\):

\[4d^2 \text{ weights, whatever } h \text{ is.}\]

So splitting into heads is free. The paper tested this (Table 3, row A). One big head scored 0.9 BLEU worse than 8 heads. Too many heads hurt as well: with 32 heads of size 16, quality dropped again. Each head needs enough numbers to ask a useful question.

Part 1’s rank argument says why. A head of size \(d_k = d/h\) can only make every possible pattern over \(n\) words if \(d_k \ge n\), that is \(h \le d/n\). Bhojanapalli et al. (2020) checked this in BERT-large (\(d = 1024\), sequences of \(n = 128\), so the limit is \(h = 8\)), keeping the weight count fixed at 336 million:

heads head size \(d_k\) SQuAD F1 MNLI accuracy
8 128 90.89 85.0
16 64 90.61 84.5
32 32 90.45 84.4

Past 8 heads, each head drops below \(n\) and scores slip. The drop is small, but it goes one way. Their fix is to stop tying the head size to \(d/h\): pick \(d_k\) by itself, at least as big as \(n\). “Free” is true for the weight count, not for what each head can express.

Further reading

  • Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need, sections 3.2.2 (multi-head), 3.5 (positions) and 4 (why self-attention).
  • Amirhossein Kazemnejad, Transformer Architecture: The Positional Encoding: a careful look at the rotation property.
  • Jesse Vig, BertViz: see what real attention heads learn.
  • Su et al., RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding (2021): section 3.4 has the derivation and the decay bound.
  • Biderman et al., Rotary Embeddings: A Relative Revolution (EleutherAI, 2021): RoPE derived with complex numbers, plus experiments.
  • Lilian Weng, The Transformer Family Version 2.0 (2023): a survey of position encodings and attention variants.

Series · Attention is all you need 1Self-attention from scratch 2Multi-head attention and positions 3One encoder block 4The decoder, masking and training 5Inference and the KV cache

In 2017 a team at Google published a paper with a bold title: Attention Is All You Need. It described the Transformer. Today almost every large language model, from ChatGPT to Claude, is built on it.

This series rebuilds the Transformer piece by piece. Every figure runs a real (but tiny) Transformer in your browser, and every number you see is computed, not drawn by hand. You can change the sentence and watch every matrix change with it.

This first part covers the idea at the heart of the paper: self-attention. In a previous post I treated the network as a black box that hands out scores. Now we open the box.

The toy model

Real models are huge: GPT-3 gives each word 12,288 numbers. Ours gives each word 8, so whole matrices fit on screen. The rest of the setup:

  • a vocabulary of about 30 words (press words it knows in the figure to see them),
  • attention with d_k = 4 numbers per query and key,
  • weights from a fixed random seed, except for one attention head that I wired by hand so it has a clear story to tell.

The model is not trained, so it can’t write a sentence. But the arithmetic is exactly the arithmetic of the paper. I checked it against PyTorch’s own Transformer layers, and they agree to within 10⁻¹⁴.
